speechtext:
The sentence referred to by my hon. friend has not been remitted. Under a statute passed last year any person convicted of an indictable offence has the right of appeal to the Court of Appeal of the province' that imposed his conviction, and this appeal must be lodged within a delay to be fixed by the rules of the Court of Appeal of such province. In most of the provinces of the Dominion such rules have been made, and the usual delay is thirty days within which an appeal may be instituted by the convict. In the province of Quebec no such rules have yet been enacted, but I am informed that steps are now being taken to enact such rules. Article 1018 of the Criminal Code as enacted last year provides:
In the case of a conviction involving sentence of death or whipping the sentence shall not in any case be executed until after the expiration of the time within which notice of appeal or of an application for leave to appeal may be given under this section.
Instructions have been issued to all the wardens of the penitentiaries by the Department of Justice that the lash shall not be inflicted until after the expiration of the delay during which the convict has the right to institute an appeal against his conviction. The message which has been sent in the case of Beauchamp was only a reiteration or confirmation of instructions which the wardens have already received from the Department of Justice. This man's sentence neither with regard to the part of it concerning the lash nor the other part, has not been remitted, and if any application has been made for clemency in this case it will be dealt with in the ordinary way.
I may perhaps add that many things have been stated either verbally or in writing which are not justified by the facts of the case.

I have a further criticism of the budget to make, and it is a very serious one. The Prime Minister and the Acting Minister of Finance were parties to the budget of last year. To be sure that budget was delivered by the Finance Minister himself (Mr. Fielding), but it expressed the will of the government and indicated what the people might expect from it in the way of a fiscal policy. That policy of a year ago is in sharp contrast to the policy as set forth in the budget of April 10. I am not anxious, Mr. Speaker, to use any harsh language, but I will state that if one will read the budget of May 11, 1923, and will place alongside of it and read the budget of April 10,	1924, he will
see that the budget that we are now considering constitutes a plain breach of good faith. I may be asked, did I expect anything else? I certainly did. I may be prejudiced, but I felt when the budget was given to the people last year, as it foreshadowed the fiscal policy of the government with relation to the tariff, that we could expect something abiding, after that address which was given so forcibly on May 11, 1923.
Honour in public life, Mr. Speaker, is an absolute necessity. It is the last thing we can part with. Honour in keeping engagements with the people has been the very breath and 
existence of public men in all British countries. A recent example of this is the action of the late Prime Minister of Great Britain, who, succeeding the Right Honourable Bonar Law, felt himself bound by a statement that the Right Honourable Bonar Law had made to the effect that there would be no material change in the fiscal policy of Great Britain without a submission to the people. A controversy was carried on at great length in the newspapers that the promise which Bonar Law had made did not constitute a binding obligation. In the next place it was stated that the Right Honourable Stanley Baldwin was not heir to that promise, or called upon in any way to implement it; but he took the position that he was not going to run any risk of imputation of bad faith whatever, and he went to the country, with the result which hon. gentlemen know; but with the result also that the good name and the good faith of public men were maintained.
How different the practice in this House! On May 11, 1923, the Finance Minister announced his fiscal policy and gave assurances as to what this policy would continue to be. Now I will say just a word with reference to the Finance Minister. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), when he was seeking office in 1921, from the public platforms practised self abnegation to this extent: "Do not look at me; look at the man whom I propose shall be Finance Minister. He was successful in the years of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and gave to this country its fiscal policy in the years of its greatest prosperity. He is the man whom I intend to have as my Finance Minister, if I am returned'to power." Since he has been returned to power we have had the opinion of the right honourable Minister of Finance, expressed by the Prime Minister in words which could be summed up by saying that he was the very flower and sweet perfume of his ministers:	That the fiscal interests of this
country Were absolutely safe in the hands of the Right Hon. W. S. Fielding. Now, I regret exceedingly-I think as much as anyone in this House 'that the right hon. Finance IMinister is not here to-day. If he were here, we never would have had, I submit, this budget, which was delivered by the Acting Finance Minister (Mr. Robb).
Let me quote what was said by the Finance Minister in his budget speech of May 11, 1923, to be found in Hansard at page 2648, and pardon me if I read at length. He said:
Tariff Stability
There is a thought which does not receive as much consideration as I think sometimes it should be given in public discussions, and that is the desirability of something like tariff stability. Business men do not

like to be always threatened with changes in the tariff. There is no finality in legislation either as respects that tariff or as respects anything else. That which parliament can do to-day it can undo to-morrow. Everybody knows that. Everybody must conduct his business in the light of that fact. Nevertheless it is desirable that something like an assurance of tariff stability should be given to business men'. Exceptions will occur. There will be cases where, in the interest of the consumer, reductions in the tariff ought to be made. There will be inequalities discovered in the tariff which should be corrected; there will be errors which should be remedied. Any minister, any government, any parliament must be free to deal with these cases as they arise. But the conditions to which I refer are exceptional. Speaking broadly, it is possible to give the country a reasonable assurance of stability of tariff. Such assurances are very desirable, for no business man would care to enter upon enterprises which may be brought into peril by frequent tariff changes. The tariff as it will be when the changes proposed to-day come into effect will be a moderate tariff and probably as low as the country can afford to have under present condition.
Then on the next page:
Subject to the exceptional conditions such as I have mentioned, I think the country should be content to accept the tariff as it will now stand as one as fair and reasonable as can be prepared under all the circumstances, and business men should be able to carry on the various enterprises without the fear of being soon disturbed by further changes.
Stability of tariff cannot be expected while tariff rates are high. But where the rates are for the most part, as in our tariff, moderate, a reasonable measure of tariff stability should be assured.
Now, Mr. Speaker, unfortunately the Finance Minister is not here, but we have another gentleman in this House this afternoon who expressed himself on this question of tariff stability and I desire to quote from his statement. This statement, instead of covering three or four paragraphs such as I have read, is spread over seven or eight columns. I will read what I have selected, and if there is anything that I have left out, I want my attention drawn to it, because I want to show this House if I can what was the attitude of the Prime Minister not twelve months ago. On page 30o2 of Hansard, I find the following statement by the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King:
May I say just a further word with respect to another feature of the budget-the emphasis which has been placed upon stability as regards the tariff in the government's tariff announcements. Why is it that the present government is seeking stability in the tariff? Eor the simple reason that what this country needs to-day, as what the world needs, is a little more in the way of stability.
That was his statement on May 23, 1923. Something has happened since. He continues:
What we need to-day is to restore a feeling of confidence in the minds of the business community, and in the minds of the industrial community. The world to-day is still trembling more or less from the convulsion of the titanic struggle of a few years ago, and the highest duty of statesmanship is to seek,

Stability does not mean finality. I notice that some hon. gentlemen oposite have sought to combine the two words.
If there was one thing above another which the hon. Minister of Finance was most careful tp emphasize when he spoke of stability, it was that as regards all legislation, and in particular as regards the tariff, there was no such thing as finality. He spoke particularly and specifically of the probable need for a change as respects some items of the tariff affecting consumers and in relation to the necessities of production.

As I have remarked-and please let this sink in there has been no change whatever except an adverse change against us since this speech was delivered by the Prime Minister of Canada in the House of Commons. He said further:
What is the position with regard to the United States? Since the Liberal convention was held, there has been enacted by the United States a much higher tariff than ever before existed between Canada and the United States. The Fordney-McCumber tariff, so-called to-day is operating to the disadvantage of Canada' Is there any member of this House who will stand up in his place and say: Notwithstanding that obvious fact we think we should throw down our bars against the United States and give them an opportunity to come in here and affect our industries in a manner even more seriously than they have already been affected.
Yes, there was a member, and that mem-bei sits opposite me to-day in the person of the Prime Minister of Canada. He said further:
We feel that the settlement of conditions in Europe and the favourable change in the American tariff are not likely to be effected for some little time yet, and for that reason we say that pending a change m this external situation we wish to give to the Canadian people the assurance that we do not purpose having an unstable tariff, because that is the significance of it. The one word has to be used in relation not only to its synonym but also its antonym. We do not propose to have an unstable tariff while this unstable condition exists in different parts of the world.
Why the change of opinion? When did the stability occur and become a fact in other parts of the world? Then on page 3053 the Prime Minister continued. I hope he is following me, and I will read any part that he suggests I should. I am anxious to have a plain, truthful account of the attitude as then expressed by the speech of May 23, 1923:
Before I leave that matter, may I add this with respect to our endeavour to bring about stability?
We are taking in this connection a stand which we believe to be not only in the interests of our own country but in the interests of the world. I have in (Mr. Ryckman.]
my hand a copy of the report which was presented to this parliament some little time ago of the Genoa Conference for the economic and financial reconstruction of Europe. Canada was represented at that conference by two able and distinguished gentlemen and there were assembled there, as hon members will recall, representatives from most of the commercial nations ot the world. True, in some respects the conference did not achieve all that was hoped and expected of it. but there were certain matters on which there was general agreement, and in the report of this conference, I find the following. It appears on page 37 of the report printed by order of this House.
Then there is given article 44 of the Genoa conference that was in favour of stability. The Prime Minister cited not only the Genoa conference but the League of Nations, and he showed how the Economic committee of the league was in favour of stability. He quoted a resolution which, in part, is as follows:
The Economic committee is deeply impressed with the inconvenience and injury caused to international commerce which result from the uncertainty arising from frequent changes of customs tariff and associates itself cordially with the resolution of the Genoa Conference on this subject.
The committee strongly recommends that all states should endeavour to ensure that their customs tariffs should remain applicable over substantial periods of time, and that changes in rates and classification should be effected as seldom as possible and only when they are required by the essential economic needs of the country.
After quoting that resolution, the Prime Minister continued:
That resolution, according to the report of the assembly, was unanimously adopted by the assembly of the League of Nations at its last session. Now I read these resolutions not for the purpose of helping to foster the impression that in speaking of stability in matters of tariff the action of the government contemplates finality in any particular or in any direction. I rather wish to bring home to the members of this House, as far as may be possible, what has become so apparent to the statesmen of other parts of the world, that if we are to get away from the unsettled conditions of the present, if we are to restore confidence among the nations of the world, if once more this world is to be brought back to the order which prevailed prior to the Great War. we must all seek, in whatever directions we can, particularly in our international ' relations, to establish something in the nature of a reasonable stability. That is all we are aiming at. We do not intend to sacrifice in any particular the needs of any class of our citizens or the needs of industry, the needs in any direction of consumers or of producers, but what we do wish to make clear is that, so long as conditions continue to exist as they are at present, so long ns on the part of the United States, the tariff wall remains what it is against us, and in Europe the unsettled condition continues to be what it is, and so long, may I add, as Canada remains the only country that has reduced its tariff since the Great War, while other countries continue to put up their tariffs, for that period of time at least we shall give to those who are interested in investing their capital and establishing industry in this country, and who are seeking to restore business to a higher level of development, assurance that there will not be unstability where stability ought to prevail.

With regard to this French treaty I want to take one article which comes under the treaty and another which does not, so that we may see how the low rate of exchange adversely affects this country. I understand that when the friends of the Acting Minister of Finance who are in the boot and shoe business were here they pointed this out to the Prime Minister and to the Acting Minister of Finance. I think this French treaty should be denounced. The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) should be kept at home unless he goes over merely to sign a treaty, or unless he leaves forthwith to have this treaty denounced. No bit of business that has been transacted, by this government dealing with expofts from and imports into this country is more worthy of condemnation from a business point of view than this treaty with France.
I desire, Mr. Speaker, to say a word or two with regard to the nuisance and pest taxes. There is a sales tax: I hope an opportunity will be given to discuss it later. But I know the members of this House feel that this tax is most unfair and discriminatory in its application to different businesses. It increases the cost of living ten per cent; there is general agreement on that point. If the government had seen fit to give the farmer the benefit in the matter of dry goods, drugs, boots and shoes-well, boots and shoes are covered-and groceries through the remission of this tax, the benefit to the farmers would have been tremendously in excess of anything they could get from the cut on agricultural implements.
I must say a word about the note tax. This tax is simply grotesque:	I wonder if members of the House have really considered what it means? I defy the Prime Minister to find such a tax anywhere else on earth, and that is a large order. How does it work? Suppose two men wish to go into business, or, if they are already in business, suppose their business needs more money. Suppose they want to put into it $200,000, one of them $100,000 and the other a similar amount. One of the men who puts in $100,000 and has the money in the bank can put on the cheque a dollar stamp. The other man has good credit; he goes to the bank and says, "I want $100,000 and I will pay you back $10,000 monthly; here is my security." He gets the loan; it goes through the bank in the ordinary way, and he pays a note tax of $220, or 220 times what the other man pays. Look at the discrimination. The man who is able to sit down and write out a cheque for that large amount might be regarded as being in a fortunate position, and if there is any saddling of tax on one of the two it should be on the man who has the money. But under this splendid taxation scheme of the Minister of Finance the situation is as I have stated it, and that condition enters into the everyday business life of this country. Anyone who borrows money
from the bank and reduces the loan by payments every month or every two or three months, as the case may be, is met with this tax, while the man who has the money to pay outright enjoys relatively no taxation.
I desire to say a word about the income tax. The member for Red Deer (Mr. Speak-man) suggested that the income tax be increased, and I heard a member sitting behind him say, "Yes, they cannot pass on the income tax." Indeed they can. The income tax increases immensely the cost of living, and just to show you that practically everybody can pass on the income tax, how does the manufacturer do it? The manufacturer says: Well, I give myself a drawing allowance of $10,000, or whatever it may be, and now that I have to pay income tax I will increase my drawing allowance so much to cover that tax, because I have to have the same amount to live on. The increase goes into the cost of the goods, and the people who buy the goods pay that increase; that is the way it is done.
We come to the merchant, and he does it in just about the same way; it is passed on in that case. Then we come to the professional classes. The professional man says:	I
have so much income tax to pay, and I will increase my charges so much to cover it; he pass.es it on, and that adds to the cost of living. Oh, but you stick the salaried man, you say. You do not, because everybody recognizes that the man who lives on a stated salary is entitled to more salary now that he has to pay income tax, and so you find our colleges and schools, our manufacturing establishments and every other concern that employs the salaried man, recognizing the fact that he needs more, giving him more, and that all adds to the cost of living.
Oh, you say, at any rate we get the man who by thrift has saved his money and invested it in stocks, bonds and mortgages. You do not get him at all. He can get out from under if he wants to do it. How does he do it? He has a mortgage say for $10,000. He will go to a lawyer and say: Draw up an assignment of half that mortgage to my wife. It is a very easy thing to do, requiring no registration. What does a man with bonds do? His wife gets some of them, and the other members of his family get some until he has reduced his liability to pay income tax to the smallest possible amount. And so through the whole list.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the income tax in the form in which we have it means that industry is paralysed, that initiative is stifled, and that business suffers tremendously. How does it work in business? Suppose there are
The Budget-Mr. Ryckman

some men who are carrying on a prosperous business, but who need more capital. They say: We have lots of security but we want to raise $250,000, we will say, and they put out a. preferred stock issue at 7 per cent. Money is hard to get; it will be a gilt-edged 7 per cent investment, and we will ask the public or our friends to subscribe. But what do they find? They know some of their friends who have money and to whom 7 per cent should be a good investment, and always predicating that there is an abundance of assets behind this proposed issue of securities, they go to their friends and say:	This is a
good 7 per cent investment; you know what it is; we ask you to take an interest in it. Oh, says the prospect, I require 7.59 per cent to pay my taxes, and I have to have an investment that will yield me 7.59 per cent, or I am far better off by buying tax-free bonds. And the industry that wants the money cannot get it. Practically every broker's office and every bond dealer's office throughout the country has printed lists showing how it would pay you, if your income is a stated amount, to invest in tax-free bonds, and the result is that there is not the money for industry. Are there any flotations to-day? Is there anybody outside of say the pulp and paper industry who knows that sinfie this government came into power there have been many investments in industry? There have not been, and everybody knows it. I would go further and say that just so long as this government is in power, just so long as they are rocking the industrial boat, just so long will there not be money for industry in Canada, and just so long will there be a crowd of men in the bond business such as we have never had before. The bond business has grown tremendously. Take the cities of Montreal and Toronto; the bond dealers there have become a distinct class in the com-munit}'-. Offices are crowded with those engaged in the bond business, and they are not selling the securities of industrial companies.
Now what is the effect of all these taxes? The net effect so far as immigration is concerned, is that we have not got it, and the reason that we have not got it is that those who are coming to a foreign country know well what that foreign country is going to do for them. They know the taxation in that foreign country; there is no question about that, and immigration to this country is stayed simply because this is one of the highest taxed countries in the world and has some of the most inequitable taxation methods anywhere in the world.

The member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) told us, and I will accept his statement because I believe it is true, that people are leaving this country because they can do better elsewhere, the taxation here being so high. The Minister of 'Justice (Mr. Lapointe) in his remarks tried to tell us that the income tax we had to pay in Canada compared favourably wTith the income taxation in Great Britain and the British colonies. True, although the Canadian scale is higher in some regions of the tax, but federal income taxation is not the only income taxation we have to pay. We have municipal income taxation, and one or two provinces impose income taxation, and there is no telling when other provinces will not have it. There are even amusement taxes, and all these other taxes that we know of, and which I shall not take up the time of the House to mention. But that is the reason why immigration to this country is stagnant. We want desirable immigrants, and we are not getting them because the fact is known to the world at large that taxation in this country, under this government, is higher than in other countries to wThich these immigrants can go.

speechtext:
I am labouring as earnestly as I can to conclude my remarks in as short a time as possible, and I do not wish to take up the balance of the session.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the farming community is not going to be influenced by this dole, which has been reckoned at $2.50. The hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Stansell) said that within his experience, and as he calculated it, it did not amount to more than $2.50. For myself I do not know how even that much is arrived at. But all industry, not only the farming industry but all industry, including, of course, and emphasizing agriculture, needs steadiness and stability, and this can only be got by getting together and by planning for the success of the whole country. The difficulty with this government is that when they go into executive session they plan how they can stay in power instead of how they can benefit the country. I would be very sorry if I thought the measure of the benefit agriculture was going to get was contained in this budget and in the tariff reductions for the benefit of the farmer. I think that agriculture has higher claims which should be recognized, and which would be recognized by any body of business men who sat down together to decide on the interests of the country and

The Budget-Mr. Ryckman
how best to ensure them, just as if they were the directors of a business organization. You will find, Mr. Speaker, that the west and the east and the centre of this great Dominion will not be satisfied with any policy which is a distinct menace to any important section' of the country. I wish to say that there is in the minds of certain people-I won't say the most important, but I do say a very important section of this country; I am referring to the manufacturing industry-the greatest unrest, disturbance, uncertainty, and perplexity, and so long as these conditions prevail the country cannot prosper.
The situation with regard to the United States troubles me very much. I am not offering what I am about to say as a solution of the whole matter, not by any means. But I frankly believe it would benefit the farmers of Canada, I am very sure it would benefit the farmers of the province from which I come, if we took a self-respecting, independent stand with regard to the United States. By that I mean this:	I never knew anyone to
get along very far in this life who had not a good measure of self-respect, who did not adhere to a straightforward policy in his own interest, and did not determine to do the best he could for himself with due regard to the rights of others. If there is a nation on earth that recognizes an upstanding man, a man of self-respect who will look after himself, it is the United States. For many years I have been interested in business in that country. Without any conceit I think I can say I know pretty well all about it, and I want to state now that nothing would condemn Canada in the minds of the people of the United States like a policy of truckling to the latter country, such as, when we have a duty of 4 cents on a particular commodity, allowing them to impose a duty of 8 cents against us. Just so soon as we make up our minds that we are going to look after our own interests, so soon will the United States respect us. But in the past we have truckled to the United States, we have lowered our duties against them, and every time we have done that they have retaliated by raising the duties against us. I am tempted to relate an incident which occurred but a short time ago. I was in the company of American gentlemen, and we were discussing the tariff. I said something like this: Canada is a new country, the United States is a big nation. We have got to have a tariff for revenue and for the protection of our industry. Why could not your country adopt a tariff with respect to us on the s&me basis as we adopt with respect to the United States? I said, "We are a young
country, you ought to do that." What reply do you think I got to that suggestion? I venture to say not one man in this House could tell me the nature of that reply. The reply was, "Canada is not a new country, Canada is just as old as the United States." Read the last number of Current History. It contains an article written by an American. He said With respect to the United States that it stayed out of the war for its own economic purposes, and that when it entered the war it did so for the same reason. Just so long as it suits the United States to place a higher tariff against Canada she will continue to carry out that policy. She will lower the tariff when it suits her and not before. I have not a word of complaint to make against the United States. She is acting in what she conceives to be her own interest, with a desire to develop business for herself, and that is a thing she has a perfect right to do. In behalf of this Dominion I ask that we also should have some national self-respect and, in the light of past experience, attend to our own business.

named by the Speaker of the House. speechtext: As a representative from the province of Nova Scotia, at the outset I desire to express my regret at the absence of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and also the hope that he will soon come back to us restored in health and vigour of mind. speechtext:
I think it is very difficult to satisfy the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), no matter what is done. I find it almost impossible for any hon. member to discuss any question in the House unless he adopts, yOu might say, the viewpoint or the standpoint of the province from which he comes. Furthermore, he is liable to discuss it from the viewpoint of the constituency he represents. There may be some weakness in this or there may not. There may be an advantage. We in Nova Scotia realize that the interests of the Dominion of Canada are far greater than our interests. We realize that Nova Scotia is a small part of the Dominion, and yet we believe that the prosperity of the part will make the prosperity of the whole, and it is only as the different parts are prosperous that the whole will become prosperous. It is difficult also to legislate for the whole Dominion, our interests are so varied, and the country so great in extent. The gold mining industry is confined to the four provinces of Canada. The fishing industry is confined mostly to the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts. Some of our provinces have not any lumbering industries. Manufacturing seems to be centered in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. There is, however, one industry that is common to the whole Dominion, and is found in every province in some form or other. That is the industry of agriculture. Therefore, it would seem to me that when the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) attempts in any way to lighten the burden of agriculture, he is legislating for the whole of the Dominion of Canada.
I desire to say, Mr. Speaker, that ever since confederation there has been more or less discontent in the province of Nova Scotia. There is no use going back to ancient history to show the cause of our discontent; but I wish to point out that there has been discontent in Nova Scotia, owing principally to the fact that we have not progressed as fast possibly as other parts of the Dominion, and I might say that our not progressing is due to a great extent to our geographic position. After confederation we attempted to develop our industries as well as we could up to the year 1878. In that year the National Policy was introduced, and we were told that in a very short time Nova Scotia would be a great country. They pointed out to us our marvellous resources, and they are marvellous. They pointed out to us that we had great shipping facilities, and we have those facilities. They pointed out that we had the winter wharves of the Dominion of Canada, and we were told that factories would spring up on all sides. We waited for some time. The people were

The Budget-Mr. Robinson
told time after time that these things would happen, but what did happen? Well, factories did spring up. We had a certain number of woollen mills, a certain number of cotton mills, boot and shoe factories and so on. After a while these were absorbed by larger companies in Quebec and Ontario and finally, when the time came for the curtailing of production, our factories were closed down and we have very few there to-day as a result of the introduction of the so-called National Policy.
I do not want to give the House the idea that we are not making any progress in Nova Scotia. WTe are making progress along certain lines. I desire to call attention to the coal production of Nova Scotia. In 1891 we produced S3,543,000 worth of coal and in 1921 the production had increased to over $27,000,000. To-day it stands at about $40,000,000. I call attention also to our fishing production. Perhaps, in order to hurry along, I might give the carefully estimated figures for the year 1923. Our figures for that year amounted to something over $11,500,000 in spite of the fact that we have the Fordney tariff against us. The farm products of Nova Scotia for 1923 amounted to $26,000,000 and the products of the forest amounted to some $12,000,000. I call the attention of the House to the fact that these are the products of the basic industries of Nova Scotia. They are the produces of mining, farming, fishing and lumbering. One other item I should call attention to is the production of iron and steel. This was virtually nothing in 1891 and has increased in 1923 to something over $12,000,000. Now if we are producing all of these goods-and we are-the question might arise, why is there discontent in Nova Scotia? I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that, it is due primarily as I have said to our geographical position.

speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. Robinson
tempt to get them reduced and we have been successful. During the war there was an embargo on the shipment of apples, which embargo was removed in 1919. During the year 1919 the rate for carrying apples from Halifax to Liverpool was $5 a barrel, but even at that rate we found that we could make a little because the price in England was good. Later on the bottom dropped out of the market, and the steamship companies found that if they did not reduce the rate we would not send any apples over, so that the result was that of their own accord tjiey reduced the rate to $3.25 a barrel. The price however, of apples continued to fall with the result that there was formed in Nova Scotia what was called a shippers' association, formed by representatives of farmers, buyers and shippers of apples, and they approached the steamship companies to find out if it would be possible to reduce the freight rate below $3.25 a barrel. The strange part of the matter is that they had to go to the city of New York in order to find out about freight rates on apples from one British port to another in a British bottom. These representatives, however, went to New York, and they met this North Atlantic Shipping Board, or whatever it is called.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: North Atlantic Conference, Eastern Board.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They met these men, and they got a reduction in the freight rate from $3.25 to $1.10 by simply threatening that if the freight rate was not reduced, they would hire Norwegian tramp steamers, fit them up as fruit boats and use them for carrying the fruit.
I am mentioning these facts simply in order to show that we have made every attempt we possibly could to get shipping rates reduced.
The next reduction that we might possibly make would be a reduction in the cost of production. The production of apples would include tilling the soil, fertilizing the soil, spraying the apples and so on, those operations that might be called agricultural operations. Of course, we cannot expect to make any reduction in wages. If we do not pay the men for doing this work as much as they can get elsewhere, they will go elsewhere to work and, therefore, we have not been able to make, prior to this time, any reduction in the cost of production. I have heard it said, over and over again, that farmers have no business sense; that if they would put as much brain power into the marketing of their goods as they do into the production of their goods, they would be able to make a profit. In Nova Scotia, we do apply brain power to taking care of the fruit and everything

in relation to it. For instance, we buy co-operatively; we buy barrels, fertilizers and spraying materials in large quantities. We have built warehouses co-operatively. We handle the fruit usually through farming companies, so that we have cut out as far as possible any overhead expenses, and yet we have so far been unable to reduce the cost of production.
I should like to mention one fact about cooperation, because I do not believe it has been sufficiently stressed in this House. I believe it is possible-in fact I know it is possible, because we have proved it in Nova Scotia as regards the fruits industry-for the farmers to do a great deal by co-operation. Last session I was a member of a special committee on agricultural conditions, and I noticed one thing, namely, that in connection with handling fruit and various other crops throughout Ontario and some of the other provinces, there was no attempt at co-operative buying or selling on the part of the farmers. One of the most interesting witnesses that we had before that committee was Professor Jackman, professor of political economy in the University of Toronto, and if I might be allowed, I should like to read a few words from his evidence along this very line. He said:
There is no question in my mind but that the present system of the individual farmer dealing with the organized groups with whom he has relations, is an out-ofdate system. The day when the farmer as,an individual can match up with the commercial structure from whom he makes his purchases, and to whom he makes his sales, is an outworn system. The farmer looking at his own particular interest has been too strongly individualistic; he is inclined to think that his individually is at stake if he merges his interests with those of others in the same line in order to form a group to handle his products. The system under which he has worked in the past proved satisfactory; the system under which he is working to-day, the system under which the individual is grouped, the organization that handles and deals in his products is out of date, and the sooner the farmer can learn that, the better it will be; the sooner the farmer can learn that his interests demand that he shall work in concert with others in the same group as himself, so that they can operate together, so that they can present a united front in buying or selling, so that they can use a collective influence, the sooner will the farmer's conditions be rectified with some degree of permanency. But so long as the conditions prevail under which the farmer works as an individual, and buys and sells as an individual, so long shall we have this present difficulty, and the more the other groups become organized the worse will be the farmer's position, unless he follows suit. Now, in the present state we are accustomed to think that supply, the inter-relation of supply and demand determines the price of the product; there is no question in regard to the operation of that principle. There is the thing which is operating against the farmer's interests. When the farmer is putting his supply on the market in the fall or during any other season, and is putting that product on as an individual, and others are doing the same, they are competing against one another, whereas these organizations with which they have to deal are acting more or less in

The Budget-Mr. Robinson
-concert. The buyers of wheat for example are acting more or less in concert, the buyers of live stock know what one another's prices are, and with these conditions prevailing and the individual farmer dealing with organizations of that kind, it simply means that the organized efforts of the group are going to bid one farmer against another, and that the man who is most anxious to sell will be the one who will take the lowest price.
I do not think there is any need to follow this further. In the province of Nova Scotia we have decided that co-operative effort on the part of the farmers is the only thing that will bring results.

speechtext:
I wish to add just a few more words to what I have already said. I have tried to show that we do make, and have made, an attempt to reduce transportation charges on apples, and we have also attempted to reduce the cost of production; and having reached the lowest possible minimum that we can get we still have to do business, so 93
that the margin is very small. The reason why the people in my constituency are more or less pleased with the budget proposals brought down by the Acting Minister of Finance lies in the fact that these proposals will result in lessening the cost of tillage, and so on, through reducing the prices of the necessary implements. Fertilizer is another important item in regard to which the budget proposals promise an improvement in agricultural conditions. The cost of fertilizer and also of spraying material being reduced, surely it can readily be understood why the constituency that I represent is satisfied with the present budget.
One word in conclusion. I have heard astonishment expressed at various times by different people that the farmers should organize politically. I have heard people almost resent the fact that there is in this present parliament a party comprised of farmers who are organized for political purposes. Personally this is nothing surprising to me. We have had preached in this country for over forty years the doctrine that it is possible for one class or industry to derive some advantage from political organization. Having had that doctrine emphasized during all that time is it to be wondered at that the agricultural interests of this country should have come to believe it after all? It is not surprising to me; and if the manufacturers can organize for political ends I do not see why the agricultural people should not. It seems to me the natural outcome and growth of the seed that has been sown during the last forty years. There may be those in this House who will say that any advantage that is gained by any class through the manipulation of the tariff up or down can be gained only at the expense of some other class. I for one believe that is right. I cannot see myself how it is possible for us to legislate a dollar into any man's pocket unless we legislate it out of somebody else's pocket. So that the best we can do is to tiy to have the least possible injury to the few and the greatest benefit to the many. I therefore favour the budget proposals because I believe that they tend to give the greatest possible benefit to the largest number while doing the least possible injury to a small fraction of the people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It would seem to me that, from the standpoint of the West, the budget undoubtedly is looking in the right direction;
and yet, as I think of the pro-5 p.m.	posals advanced, I cannot see
that they go very far towards relieving the ordinary citizen of the burdens

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

which are now imposed upon him. It is stated that the budget has been balanced, but I think that anything like a study of the budget itself must reveal the fact that this balancing is more apparent than real. Without discussing that point, however, I would suggest that in so far as it is balanced, it is at a very heavy cost. There has been a cutting-down of certain important services: we have seen the elimination of the agricultural grant and a reduction in the estimates for public health, services which surely ought to be maintained and extended at this time. On the other hand, however, there has been a continuance of the taxation levied on the poorer people involving very considerable privation in a great many homes throughout the country. The necessities of life are still taxed notwithstanding a large measure of unemployment; and what is perhaps the most serious phase of the whole situation, from the national point of view, we face the continued migration of large numbers of our people to the United States. It was stated the other day that over 100,000 of our returned men are now living in the United States. Surely nothing more significant than that could be said to indicate the unfortunate position in which this country finds itself to-day. A few years ago these men went overseas to fight for their country and they returned only to find that that country had no room for them. In my speech on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne I outlined some of the positions which we as a labour group took in regard to the general conditions of the country to-day. I should like to run over these very briefly to-day to illustrate some of the points upon which I have not so far had time to enter.
We have an enormous national debt, with its heavy interest charges; that has recently been very graphically set forth in a leaflet issued by the council of the Montreal Board of Trade. Last year I think I gave the figures for Winnipeg and the province of Manitoba; as a variation let me give these for the province of Quebec and for the city of Montreal. The public debt-Dominion of Canada debt and guarantees-has risen since 1913 from $98 per capita to $387 per capita. Adding the debts of the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal, the total of the different items per capita has risen from $241 in 1913 to $612 in 1923. It means that a family of five now owe $3,060, and a family of ten, $6,120; and, as this leaflet points out, "whether they know it or not, they are being taxed for it in high prices." That is what makes it necessary for

some of us to urge a more radical change than the government has seen fit to make in the tariff at this time.
Let me refer to the income tax returns. We had a net total from individuals in 1922 of almost $40,000,000 and in 1923 of only some $32,000,000; from corporations in 1922 of over $39,000,000 and in 1923 of less than $29,000,000. This past year we raised all told only $60,000,000 from the income tax, a very considerable reduction on that which was raised the year before. The income tax at present seems to bear heavily upon the very large number of people of comparatively small resources, yet we find that the banks are able to declare large dividends fairly constant from year to year, and that notwithstanding the 'considerable bungling which certain failures have revealed. We further find that the railways, under the regulations of the Railway Commission, are practically guaranteed high dividends. The questions naturally arise why the railway and the banks should continue, whether the country is in a poor condition or not, to draw and to be practically guaranteed their returns when considerable numbers of people engaged in industry of various kinds have no such guarantee and in fact are losing steadily, and when large numbers of working people are having their wages forced down.
In connection with this income tax, I should like to point out the amounts that people outside of Canada have invested in our country. It has been estimated' recently by several very competent authorities that Americans own something like $2,750,000,000 of assets in Canada. Britishers own something like $2,250,000,000 worth and other outside investors around $250,000,000. Putting the returns at 5 per cent, thrft would mean that this country must pay a tribute to outsiders of something like $262,500,000. The question arises as to why some of these incomes which are spent outside of Canada should not be taxed. In fact I should like to go further and say, why should there not be a supertax on incomes spent outside of Canada? I notice that some of those who are most urgent in their demand that everyone should pay the tax here in this country frequently travel across for the holiday seasons or for all the winter months to the United States and thus escape the indirect taxation which must be paid by those who must remain here twelve months of the year. Undoubtedly there is a great deal of injustice in the present arrangement. With hundreds of thousands of Canadians going to the United States, and with what has been called the economic conquest of Canada-that is,

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
the increasing foreign investments in Canada-I have wondered just what advantage there is in continually harping upon the old policies and uttering the old war cries. Take for example, the following paragraph from Sir John Willison's pamphlet some years ago on the programme of the Canadian Reconstruction Association-he represents the Tory position:
We must either manufacture the raw materials of Canada, within the country-thus employing labor, rearing new communities, providing local markets for merchants and producers, strengthening the national structure, making the back of Canada strong to bear its accumulating burdens-or the sons of Canada will follow these raw materials out of the country, establish themselves in foreign industrial centres, and, more and more, from year to year, the national burden will become heavier and the issue of the great political experiment in which we are engaged become more difficult and uncertain. Every sound economic and natural reason, therefore, demands that the raw material of Canada shall be manufactured in Canada, and the Canadian people protected in the possession and control of their natural inheritance.	[DOT]
Might I suggest that all which was in that article prophesied as likely to happen if protection were abolished has actually happened within the last few years. A good deal of it would have happened even under free trade. The fact is we must get down below either protection or free trade to some more fundamental policy if we would meet the needs of the present hour. As it is, the natural inheritance of the people has been forfeited; we find a very large part of our natural resources in the hands of outsiders. Ar 1 here I should like to refer to what I might term the bogus patriotism which is frequently brought forward in an effort to influence people's minds with regard to certain fiscal policies. During the war the hoardings of my own city of Winnipeg were placarded with big posters reading something like this: " Be patriotic"; "Keep the home fires burning"; " Buy Canadian coal." I remember at that particular time making some investigations as to the nationalities of those who were engaged in mining coal in the western area, and I found that, if I remember, some 70 per cent of them were Austrians, technically our alien enemies, and that a very considerable part of the coal measures was held by American syndicates. " Be patriotic; buy Canadian coal "; and all the time what we were actually doing was paying wages to the Austrian miners and dividend's to the American mine owners. I have nothing against either Americans or Austrians, but why should we be deluded by these bogus patriotic cries. I was rather interested in an article which appeared just the other day 93i
in the New York Nation-an article which has been commented upon by some of our Canadian papers but, which I think, has not been answered. This is entitled " Economic Conquest of Canada" by Scott Nearing, in the number of April 16:
The present economic policy of Great Britain is compelling American capitalists to take a larger and larger share of their production business into Canada. The General Motors, for example, from its plant in Ontario exported 18,000 cars in 1922. For at least one month within the past year British imports of motor cars from Canada exceeded in number and value imports from the United States. The reason is apparent. The British government collects a duty 1/6 less on Empire manufactures than on foreign manufactures. This extends in the case of automobiles to those which are 60 per cent built in Canada. The American manufacturer by locating a plant in Canada can thus supply the Canadian market free of duty and undersell his United States competitor in the markets of Great Britain.
Should the British Empire raise a higher tariff barrier with the aid of imperial preferences, United States capital will be compelled to locate a still larger proportion of its plants in Canada. Thus British imperialism is laying the foundations for American control of the strategic economic advantages of Canada.
As the American Economist sums up that part of the situation:
American capital is year by year obtaining a more complete grip of Canadian manufacturing and commercial business. Branches of large United States corporations are being established in Canada, or Canadian corhpanies are being taken over, at a rate that indicates economic conquest.
What advantage is it to us if these factories are located here, if the profits are enjoyed by people who live outside the country, and the regulations which we make in this country force wages down below the rates that prevail south of the line? I refer to the high taxation, all of which results in the transference of wealth from the many to the few. I am quite well aware that a statement of mine on this subject will not be of any very considerable value, hence I would like to quote a statement of an economist of recognized standing, Mr. J. A. Hobson, whoe in speaking of this point says:
This world war, destructive as it was, did not leave the world, as a whole, seriously diminished in its economic resources. It did not, even in Europe taken as a whole, so seriously reduce our productive resources as to make a long spell of poverty and recoupment inevitable. Almost all the economic cost of the war was defrayed out of the current real income of the world.
And again:
The connection between the inflation which the governments and banks conspired to produce and the magnitude and ownership of the war debt is not obscure. The "money" which the governments got by printing notes, by borrowing from banks, or by inciting banks to give credit to customers in order to increase subscriptions to war loans (all pure inflation), they spent in buying goods and services. Thus prices and profits mounted up the faster, because this easy way of getting

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
money made governments more careless in the rates they paid for what they bought. The immense and rapid profits-due to the expanding prices, with a lag of wages and a virtual elimination of competition- the recipients invested in war loans, the only authorized and available investment.
Again:
At the end of the depression, virtually the whole of the debt will be held by the well-to-do classes, forming a considerable reduction in the proportion of the current income of the nation available as purchasing power for the working classes.
In discussing this question of the ownership of our war debt, the Toronto Globe recently quoted Mr. A. E. Ames as stating that:	[DOT]
On January 1, 1924, out of a total national debt of $2,516,000,000 not less than $1,969,000,000 was held in Canada, and only $546,000,000 in other countries.
Now the question I should like to ask is why should large numbers of Canadians be forced year by year to pay tribute to a comparatively small group of Canadians who profiteered during the war or made profits since the war and as a result of the war. Viscount Milner speaking of the war debts has this to say:
As regards that portion of the national debt which we owe to ourselves I do contend that it does not represent a diminution of our total national wealth, but a redistribution of it between individuals. It (the national debt) is an almost intolerable embarrassment to the government, which has perpetually to extract money from a great number of people in order to put it into the pockets of a much smaller number.
Sooner or later we shall have to face the handling of our great war debt in an altogether different way from what we have done in the past. People do not like to hear talk of repudiation. People are very fond of saying that we must keep all our agreements in regard to tax-free bonds, and so on, but why should the great majority of the people of this country have to suffer year after year in order to pay tribute to the very small group of those who hold the major part of the wealth of the country to-day? May I venture to say that three kings rule in Canada to-day: Privilege, Property and Precedent, and until these are dethroned the people can expect very little relief indeed.
I speak of the burden of the overhead charges which is crippling industry and commerce. I remember this being brought to my attention some years ago, when in the West we were in the full tide of our real estate speculation. As I went into a small town in western Canada I was met at the station by a friend of mine who had a very fine automobile. It was just when automobiles were becoming common. I said, "How did you manage to make enough out of your business to buy this?" He was running a comparatively small business. He said, "I

did not make this out of my business. In fact, this ear did not cost me anything." "Well," I said, "You had better let me in on that kind of a deal." He replied, "I had a few thousand dollars to spend, and I managed to make the first payment on a lot down-town. A few weeks later the lot had increased greatly .a value, and a man offered me $2,000 on my bargain, and I took it. I had $2,000 to the good, easy money, and I suppose easy money was easily spent. I invested in the car. So you see it cost me nothing." It occurred to me at that time, if it cost him nothing, whc paid the bill? There was a good car, good materials, good workmanship and all that kind of thing. Who paid the bill? He confessed that he did not. I venture to suggest that every man who built a house on that lot, or who rented the house after it was built on that lot, helped to pay that bill, that every customer who bought his groceries from the store built on that lot helped to pay the bill. It was a perpetual charge on the productive activities of the community. What is true of real estate is true of these many mergers we have had, from the Canada Cement up or down; it is true of Besco Steel, and similar corporations with what we commonly know as watered stock.
We find that constantly, whether in government affairs or in private business, we are told that fixed charges must have the right of way. I would like some day to see that statement successfully challenged. Why should those who have managed to secure a very heavy mortgage on the country always have a prior claim when other people are suffering? We need to have some revision of our ideals on this matter. I know of no reason other than that advanced by our legal fraternity, who are working largely on precedent, why the poorer people should always have to turn over the greater part of what they make to people who have thus legally or illegally secured mortgages on all their property and the results of their labour.
I think I need not mention here-I adverted to it on a former occasion-that agriculture to-day is in a deplorable condition largely owing to the tariff, high freight rates and inadequate credit facilities. My farming friends have been portraying that condition last year and again this year to the House. As a city man I do not come into quite such direct contact with this question as those in the rural districts, but those of us who live in the cities of the West, which are so directly dependent upon the farming operations cannot but be thoroughly cognizant of the bad conditions which exist at the present time.

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
I had a letter a day or two ago from which I should like to read an excerpt with regard to a new farmers' organization which is working along very radical lines. This is the extract :
We were 700 strong last July. Now we are climbing to the 20,000 mark.
I am travelling around in this province, and I know the conditions here pretty well.
The whole province is in a state of bankruptcy.
By the way, he is speaking of Saskatchewan, not of Alberta.
Then he goes on to say:
Farmers can no longer be fooled. They know that the bankers have a monopoly over the medium of exchange which governs all commodities. They know that an army of customs officers up the coast lines and across this vast continent and in the interior are millstones on their necks. The government is legislating into the hands of a few the honest earnings of the masses. We know of the watered stocks, and of the railways which are robbing the honest farm workers- women, children and all. We know that the interlocked bankers and like industries-steel trusts, milling companies, packing houses and transportation corporations are the Shylocks.
Now, I am not saying whether that is extravagant language or not, but I do say that very large numbers of people across this country are coming to feel that way, and this is a matter which the government cannot afford to ignore. I spoke of the unemployment resulting from a lack of producing power sufficient to absorb production. I wish I could induce the members of this House to read a recent book by the authority I quoted a few moments ago, Mr. J. A. Hobson. Mr. Hobson is not a Socialist; he may be perhaps termed a radical-Liberal. He is one of the men who has been appointed by the present government in London to investigate, together with a number of financial authorities and experts, the incidence of taxation in England. In his book on the Economics of Unemployment he says that the fundamental trouble to-day is that we have had altogether too much saving of a kind. Owing to the unequal distribution of the world's wealth, a comparatively small number of people have been able to retain as their own the greater part of what has been produced. In this respect Mr. Hobson is simply carrying out the thesis which was proposed by Mr. Maynard Keynes several years ago. This accumulated wealth, which could not be consumed by the people who owned it, had to be invested; it had to be put into fixed capital, and so there came to be an undue proportion /of the annual production invested in fixed capital. That was all very well as long as the earning was confined to Great Britain, or confined to a few of the European countries, but as the development of the machine went forward and the organization of capital became more
complete we had production on a large scale in almost every country of the world, including the great oriental countries. And so we have the anomaly to-day of goods being produced in enormous quantities, quantities that are too great for the purchasing power of the people, and in some way or another, he points out, we shall have to have a more equitable distribution, or if not that at least in some way, we must ensure that a large proportion of the annual output finds its way to the great mass of the people either in the form of services or wages. Now, this is an economic theory that, perhaps, is novel to a great many who have not studied the question, and yet one that is being endorsed by a growing number of economists who are regarded, at least in the Old Country, as safe and sane. We may ask ourselves whether we ought not to take action in this House more along the newer lines of thinking and less along the lines of economists who lived in the early days of the capitalist era.
Can Canada successfully compete with the mass production of the United States? I venture to say that she can only by lowering her wages, and that in return would result in less purchasing power in this country. Can the Canadian farmer compete with the lower standards existing to-day in southern Europe? I doubt it very much. They can do so only by lowering their standards to those of Europe. This is the world situation which we must face.
I have already referred to the continued emigration of our people from this country. In connection with it, what we ought to recognize is, that in this turnover of immigrants which is being helped by the railroads, and which is, of course, an advantage to them, we are witnessing a substitution of one class of people for another class-a substitution to no small extent of the city-bred people of Great Britain and the peasant people of southeastern Europe for the native born, sturdy Canadians whom we had in this country a generation ago. For whose advantage? Not for the advantage of the majority of the people in Canada. Not for the advantage of the people who are coming over here-at least they will not get the results, although their children may. Primarily it is for the advantage of the railway and other transportation companies. We labour men have sometimes been charged with blocking the immigration policy. We have done all that we could in this part of the House to discredit certain immigration policies which were proposed by the government last year. And we will be glad to do that again if these policies are brought for-

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
ward once more. But I do not think we can be said to be taking an altogether negative attitude; I would be quite willing to advocate an immigration policy if I might be allowed to outline some of the elements which must enter into such a policy. I would say, first of all, that there should be an expropriation of vacant lands across the country, so that the settlers of to-morrow would have in principle the same position as the settlers of yesterday, that is that they would not have the burden of payments on lands that have been largely held by speculators. We should relieve the immigrants of the burden of taxation just as we advocate should be done in the case of our own people. We would advocate the use of the railroads for the people. If the railroads could not pay and do the work we would say, "Do the work anyway." That is what is urged now in regard to the farmers-that they ought to produce whether they can produce at a profit or not. I would say further that we ought to insist that in some way cheap credits should be supplied. If our present banking system is primarily for commercial needs and not for industry, then we ought to either revise it or institute another system that will be fitted primarily for the producers of this country. We ought to develop our markets, to increase the purchasing power both at home and abroad; and above all we should provide for the social welfare of the settlers. In many parts of the West one whole generation has been sacrificed in order that certain people might profit by the inflation of land values. I remember a few years ago, when I had something to do with investigating conditions in the three prairie provinces, I made a proposal to the then premier of one of those provinces for the institution of a closer community plan by which education, and medical service, and expert advice along agricultural lines would be brought within reach of the settlers. The Premier said to me "That is all very well and very laudable, but how would you finance such a scheme"? I suggested to him that a very few cents additional tax per acre on wild lands would very easily finance the whole proposition. He threw up his hands.
" Why " he said, " already the American investors are squealing because of our wild lands tax." This simiply means that the premier of that province was carrying on the affairs of that province in the interests of the American investors who came here to put money in the land at, say 810 an acre, hold it till it rose to 825 an acre, and get away with the proceeds. The premier was not carrying on the affairs 
of the province in the interests of the bona fide settlers who were putting their very life blood into the building up of our Canadian citizenship.
I referred to the instability of our banks, and I do not wish to more than mention that at this juncture. We were told the other day by the Montreal papers that we ought to carry out in the most rigid form a sentence of 25 years and lashes in the case of a bank robber. I ask in all seriousness, what about the penalty for the officials who have wrecked a great many homes in this country? I think I may say that a great many people across the country are asking such questions, and the government ^s not going to be let go scot free unless it takes very drastic action with regard to those who are looting the people's funds on a larger scale than the bank robbers so-called ever had the opportunity of doing.
I spoke of still another matter, the concentration of economic power in the hands of small groups who are able to direct the policy of industry for their own financial gain rather than towards supplying human needs. Now this is not the place to enter upon a discussion of our present money system, but I would urge that, since money is the measure of all things, the quantity of money in circulation determines the value of the money unit. I use the word money in the sense used by the Hon. Reginald McKenna. Money for him is all currency in circulation among the public and all bank deposits drawable by cheque. At the present time the control of all our moneys-we have not a great deal of gold to-day, but all our paper money and our cheque money, because the cheques perform the function of money-is vested in the hands of banks, with very small supervision indeed by the government. That means that the bankers by inflation and deflation can cause a rise and fall in the price of all commodities, and thus really levy a tax on the people, without the people having any idea how severely they are being taxed. I believe that some of the Progressive members of parliament recently visited the reversible falls at St. John. The water at these famous falls flows one way during a part of the day, and during another part of the day flows the other way; and it has been long thought that perhaps some time the tide of the bay of Fundy might be used on a very large scale for providing power. I would say that the banks have anticipated any such action as that with regard to financial affairs, and with them it is a case of " Heads I win and tails you lose." They are able, whether it is inflation or deflation, to manage to get their part of what is vulgarly known as the rake-off. Through the

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
interlocking directors undoubtedly, as we pointed out last year, this control is centred in the hands of a very small group. I do not propose to go into any details in regard to the solution. Our natural resources fundamentally belong to the people and they should be taxed until they are forced out of private hands.
I think of our great water powers across the country which are capable of electrifying our railroads and of supplying power for our homes if they could be brought into effective use. Our great coal lands have been leased to private corporations, and these corporations have been carrying forward their business with almost entire disregard either of the welfare of their workmen or of the public at large.
We spoke of the necessity of in some way bringing plant equipment under co-operative and democratic management, thus providing more abundantly for the needs of the people. There has been a very great outcry echoed in this House two years ago against the policy of "Go slow," "ca'canny," or "strike on the job," but I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that when a railroad fails to carry goods unless it can do so at a certain profit, or when the manufacturer closes down his plant unless he can keep it going at a certain profit, he is doing precisely the same kind of thing as the labour man when he says, "If I cannot work at a certain wage, then I am not going to give my service," He is sabotaging. He is reducing production. I think I have heard some of my farmer friends say in private- I hope they will not think I am giving them away-that the only possible thing for the farmers to do is to go slow on the job, produce less, and thus bring the people generally to time. It is the same policy precisely. Looked at in the large, the policy is anti-social. In the case of the railroads and the banks the anti-social effects are undoubtedly much greater in magnitude. To-day we must remember that there is no such thing as private ownership of property. Since we produce collectively in all our larger industries, we must recognize more and more that no one can absolutely say with regard to a huge plant or a large railroad, "This is distinctively my business and I will brook no interference." Rather we must remember that we are advancing to a condition in which the public will claim a very real part in the carrying on of the process of production.
My last point in the analysis of the situation which I made was the necessity of basing our foreign trade policy and international relations on a clear recognition that the world has become an economic unit in which the welfare of each nation is dependent upon the welfare of all others. I venture to say that
the movements which are going on in southeastern Europe to-day, the proposals which are being put forth by the Dawes commission, the possible change of government in France after the next election, are far more vital to the people of western Canada than are the proposed changes in our tariff. We cannot imagine that we are going to solve our problems simply by looking at the situation immediately round about us. World affairs have become so inextricably intertwined, that we must do our share in helping to solve the world's problems, if we would solve those problems close at hand. I was very much interested a few weeks ago in noting that the farmers of the western States were beginning to realize the necessity for action along this line.
The Emergency Foreign Policy Conference of American producers urged the adoption by the American government of a vigorous foreign policy designed to fulfil America's obligations as embodied in her war aims. The main points in the programme are, we are informed, the following:
1.	Establishment' of reparations within the capacity
of Germany to pay, with or without the participation of France.	_
2.	Two-year moratorium to enable Germany to stabilize her government and industry.
3.	Opposition to continued military occupation by foreign troops of the Ruhr and other invaded territory.
4.	Sympathetic encouragement and support of the democratic German republic and of the trade union and co-operative organizations which are opposed to the restoration of militarism in Europe.
5.	Opposition to international armament rivalry in construction of airplanes, submarines and poison gas, with the consequent increase in tax burdens upon the people.
0. Congressional appropriation for immediate relief for starving populations in Central Europe.
I would venture to suggest that something along this line might very well be adopted by our Canadian government. .The lack of purchasing power in Europe cuts off our market there. The low standards in England or the low standards in Europe render it impossible for us to compete except by adopting similarly low standards. We were urged the other day to exclude the Chinese from the west coast; but so long as we continue to receive goods from China or Japan or other oriental countries, undoubtedly we are faced with the fact that we must compete with the Chinese who are resident over there. If ships cannot be repaired well enough or cheaply enough in Vancouver, they are taken over to China to be repaired by orientals. We must recognize the fact that to-day we face a new situation. I should like to	suggest that we	are
children of the pioneers. Our forefathers
i460

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
came into a new world several generations ago and were able to overcome all sorts of difficulties to them entirely novel. We, their children, face another new world. In the closing chapter of his book on the History of Mankind, Mr. Van Loon suggests a very apt comparison. He says that the ship of state might be likened to an old sixteenth-century sailing vessel. Gradually through the years the old sailing vessel has been made over until she has to-day been converted into a thorough-going, first class liner. The sails are gone; the motive power is now in the hold; the sailors have been taken off the rigging and put into the stokehold. They do not altogether like the new position even though it may be less dangerous than that up in the rigging. But he suggests that the fundamental trouble with the ship of state to-day is that the old captain and the old crew are still in charge, and the old charts and the old regulations still hang in the cabin. There is the trouble to-day. We need men with a new vision. We need to work out new theories of government and new regulations if we are to be able to sail the high seas of to-day with any measure of safety.
This numerically small Labour group has difficulty often in expressing its viewpoints. Very often the older groups or parties put forward a resolution, and we are forced to vote for or against it even although such resolution may not express what we believe or its negation accomplish what we want.
I venture to suggest an amendment to the budget. I do so because I believe that, in many respects, although some of us advocate theories that seem to be very radical in their character, a very considerable number of the members of this House, especially members on the Progressive side, are quite willing to travel a long way in our direction if they are quite sure that we are not advocating anything that is immediately impracticable. So I have tried to draft a resolution in such a form that it will be found to be quite within the range of practical politics. I beg leave to move:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
Whereas the budget proposals would seem to indicate the recognition by the government of the necessity for a fiscal policy designed to encourage industries based upon the development of the natural resources of the country, and to afford some alleviation of the financial burden, bearing upon the people;
And whereas the condition of such industries and the position of consumers in general is such as to demand relief;
Therefore, be it resolved that the best interests of Canada will be served by an immediate and substantial reduction in the tariff on the necessaries of life, including foodstuffs, clothing and building materials; 
And further, that the loss of revenue, if any, which might result from such reduction in customs duties should be made good by:
(a)	The readjustment and extension of the income tax to bear more heavily on unearned incomes.
(b)	A direct tax on unimproved land values, including all natural resources;
(c)	The institution of a graduated inheritance tax on large estates.
