subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire at the begining of the few remarks I have to make on the budget to extend my sympathy to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in that he has been prevented by illness from occupying his seat in the House during this session and delivering the budget speech as we have been accustomed to hear it delivered for so many years past. But though we all regret his absence we have been fortunate in the choice of an Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), who has delivered a clear, short, substantial and unassailable budget speech. That budget speech has pleased the public at large; it has brought joy and happiness to the rank and file of the Liberal party, but I am afraid, Sir, that it has been looked upon as a thunderbolt from the blue sky of the Tory party in this House and outside of it.

The Buget-Mr. Gauvreau
Sir, * since this government came into power, the Conservative party, and the reptile press that supports them, have assailed the ministry with vituperous denunciations, because, as they used to shout, they deceived the people of this country by not living up to the promises of the platform of 1919.
You are my witness, Mr. Speaker, that in this House, since 1922, our friends to your left, the loyal opposition, one after the other, have waxed indignant over the fact that the Liberal government had not the courage to apply, while on the government benches, the principles they put forward while in opposition.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman says, "hear, hear." Perhaps he wants to occupy a conspicuous position on the Chinese wall of protection. Well, I leave that to him; he is welcome to it. I would rather be with those who want a reduction of taxes in this country.
But, strange to say, Sir, the moment a Liberal budget is brought down, in which Liberal doctrines and Liberal principles are put into effect, you hear from the same corner the other song, that we are going to ruin the country by killing our best industries. No surprise in that, as far as the Liberals-the true and unselfish Liberals- are concerned; it is the role and duty of an opposition to criticise the government, even at the risk of being accused of inconsistency, and in the face of what we have already heard, I am satisfied that in spite of the cries of the Conservative birds of the capital, this country will continue to prosper, its industries will find their activities not interfered with, and the consumer will enjoy better life, while the industries of agriculture, fishing, mining and lumbering will expand to the great benefit of the mass of the population.
It is very pleasant, Sir, to see the Liberal party going forward and leaving behind it the Tory forces, whose politics are negative of all that a nation desires in order to prosper and be happy and contented.
The hon. gentleman who was Minister of Finance in the Tory government (Sir Henry Drayton) tried to place this government in opposition to what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) said last session about the stability of the tariff. He read to this House just that part of the budget speech of 1923 which suited his purposes, but he carefully avoided reading what I consider to be essential to prove that the Minister of Finance was not a man to be caught by any
claptrap coming from any quarter whatever. It is because he knew that in a country like ours basic industries would need at some further date to be dealt with, that he said in his speech then:
There will be cases, where, in the interest of the consumer, reductions in the tariff ought to be made. There will be inequalities discovered in the tariff which should be corrected; there will be errors which should be remedied. Any minister, any parliament must be free to deal with these cases as they arise.
He had foreseen that, based on our Liberal platform, a policy of reduction would follow after some time, and it is through this open door on the tariff question that our present government has thought fit and proper to act and to act wisely.
And, Sir, throughout this country, apart from the big interests concerned, a wave of enthusiasm has prevailed since the budget has come down. From the sea east, to the sea west, the people at large are willing to admit that it is a sound policy, a national one which has at heart the welfare of the great mass of the workingmen as well as people in every walk of life. How could it be otherwise when the budget lightens the burden of taxation by reducing the net debt of Canada by $30,000,000, while taxation is reduced by $24,000,000 this year? The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) was right in saying:
It is confidently expected that this reduction will give such impetus to trade that it will result in greater development and prosperity to all the provinces of Canada.
And with this approval, in spite of the attacks from behind and from the opposition benches, the government must go forward, joining hands with the majority of the people who were crying for a change, and who have got it at last.
Now, Sir, if on the one hand, I am prepared to congratulate the government upon its Liberal policy, on the other hand, I must warn it not to forget that while we need economy in the public service and a close supervision of every department, as far as expenses and personnel are concerned, public works must not go by the board for the sake of curtailing expenditures. .
It is all very well to build branch lines especially when we see the Canadian Pacific Railway placing bonds on the market for twelve millions of dollars in order to start on a policy of extension and development; and I am not averse to helping our National Railways which are showing such good and efficient results under the management of a reliable and competent man like Sir Henry Thornton, but on the other hand, Sir, I want to see our wharves, our ports, our rivers, and
The Buget-Mr. Gauvreau

our public buildings, kept in good order and repair. I am sorry to say, that we are refused some necessary works which will cost more in repairs later on than if we do them just now. I will go so far as to say that we should sanction a certain amount of necessary expenditure on public buildings.
Take the case of Trois Pistoles in my own riding. The post office and the customs and excise offices are located in the city hall of the town of Trois Pistoles, paying rent to the city.
Now that the department is advised that the town needs the whole building for its own purposes, and the Department of Public Works has to go somewhere else for shelter, I think, Sir, it is the opportune time, for the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) to place in the estimates an amount sufficient to erect a suitable building for the above-mentioned offices-post office and customs, at Trois Pistoles.
Another point to which I desire to call the attention of the government, and especially the careful consideration of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low) is the communication that should be established between the north shore and the mainland, below Quebec. Since the crossing between Murray Bay and Riviere-Ouelle has been dispensed with, there is no communication between the two shores, from Quebec to Trois Pistoles, a distance of more than 130 miles.
All that part of the north shore, from Malbaie to Bersimis, with a population of more than twenty thousand people, is left without communication with the south shore or mainland, except during the season of navigation by sailing vessels.
It is a problem the government should have at heart to solve, and the sooner it is solved the better. These people pay taxes like the rest of us, but are deprived of all facilities for their commerce and industries.
It would cost very little to grant money to a company which will put a boat under commission to give these people communication with the south shore, especially in those hard months after the closing of navigation.
We have had in years past, a ferry boat for winter navigation between Riviere-du-Loup and Tadoussac and Escoumains on the north shore. It was a success and a benefit to the people on both coasts, but unfortunately the Conservative party while in power, for petty partisanship, caused the service to fall to the ground. I hope the government will see that this service is restored so that the population on the north -shore, isolated from the rest of the world for so many
	.
months during the winter season, may be relieved of a great hardship not understood by those in more favoux-ed places who enjoy efficient transportation.
Now there are complaints in regard to the National Railways which should be aired in the presence of the Minister of Railways so that he may help us in securing justice. First of all, I find that the management is not dealing fairly with the employees, in not bringing down at once a new pension fund. There is to-day in operation the relief and pension fund of the old Intercolonial railway employees but it is inadequate to meet conditions under the present cost of living. The minimum of pension is $30 a month, a paltry sum which is not sufficient for a man with a family to live on. Working men on the government railway should be better treated, and the sooner a new pension fund is created the better it will be for the whole system. I can assure the minister that all the men interested are willing to contribute a higher sum annually to the new fund, provided they receive a better pension when they retire from the service.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What pension are the
men receiving now?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Intercolonial Pension Fund is the only one which exists at present. I was told by the minister that a new scheme for the whole system is in course of preparation but really think they are taking too much time in formulating a plan which will be satisfactory to all concerned.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
know that men who worked on the Intercolonial for seventeen years were discharged in 1911 without any pension?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, the story is so
bad that it would take two years to outline it in detail, and I do not want tonight to occupy an undue amount of the time of the House.
I must also complain about the service in the county of Temiscouata, which I have the honour to represent in the House. For example, stations like St. Eloi and St. Arsene, where a business amounting to $100,000 a year is transacted, are left to the care of one man alone. The station agent, after working eight hours a day, from 8 a.m to 4 p.m., closes the doors, and the public arriving or going out on the evening train are left in the dark to themselves; there is no one to help with their baggage, and there is no shelter from inclement weather. Over a

The Budget-Mr. Dickie
month ago I sent complaints to the proper officers, but up to now nothing has been done to remedy the evils complained of, and I beg to call the serious attention of the Minister of Railways to these facts so that he may cause some steps to be taken for the better treatment of our population, especially in the two parishes above mentioned.
I should like also to deal with the methods employed on the Canadian National Railways in connection with investigation. I will give an example of what I mean. Some time ago accusations were brought against a certain station agent in Temiscouata. The accuser was prepared to submit his case, supported by proofs, to the commissioner appointed by the government. But, Sir, the accused was examined, although not put under oath, and in the absence of the accuser denied everything alleged against him. As a consequence he went scot-free. Another case, and a recent one, had reference to the conduct of a Levis man named Levesque. This man was accused of having used liquor while on duty and was dismissed. The investigation took place but in the absence of the accused who had asked, but with no success, to be allowed to attend with his witnesses. This man sued the National Railway board and Chief Justice Le-mieux has given judgment in which he declares the dismissal was unjust and unwarranted. The result was that the railway board were condemned to pay $2,000 to the man who had been dismissed without his case being heard at all. I can cite many instances of the same character.
May I be permitted to say that that is not the way to administer justice on the Canadian National Railways. Are we going to allow the interests of the employees to remain in the hands of those who have shown they are animated neither by justice nor fair play?
In conclusion allow me to read a few lines which may be interesting to the two old-time parties, the Liberals and the Tories:
The Conservative opposition will, of course, fight the government's proposal to reduce the taxation on Canadian industry, where such reduction means the lowering of the protectionist tariff. There may be some sniping of leaders, too, from behind the Liberal front line. But the government has nothing to fear from a straight contest on the tariff issue.
Against the Conservative policy of negation, the Liberals show, at least', some intention of going forward. It is an uphill fight, handicapped as the government is with the burdens of debt which have been fastened upon the country in years of frenzied finance. But the prospects of a real battle for progress should stir Liberal enthusiasm, and enlist the support of like-minded people, by whatever party name they call themselves.
The Conservative opposition has been magnified out of all proportion in the present parliament, very largely owing to the policy of the government in marking time instead of going forward with the mandate which the country gave to the Freer Traders in 1921. When the time for the next general election comes, even though all the resolutions of the national Liberal convention have not been enacted into legislation, a session of genuine effort to deliver the goods would place the Liberals in a more favourable light. The people of Canada are in the mood for trying something, anything rather than to stagnate, or to keep going round in the vicious circle of timid futility.
Even though the Conservative party were able to line up all the reactionary interests in the country to elect another Conservative government, it would avail them nothing. Canada must go forward, along liberal lines.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is
pleasant indeed to hear from members on the other side of the House of the prosperity of Canada under Liberal rule. Several of them have referred to that. I have not noticed though that there is any congestion of passenger traffic at our international boundary line of people coming from the United States back to Canada again. However, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) has not spoken yet and possibly we may hear from him of the return of some of our people from the south. Were I a bigoted political partisan, I would say that I am pleased with this budget speech, because I am quite sure that a wave of resentment will sweep across Canada in consequence of the action of the government at this time. However, being a Canadian I can only confess to a feeling of sorrow that the great Liberal party should at last capitulate to the free trade element of the country, because that is what it means.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hope the hon.
gentleman is right.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
An hon. gentleman says he hopes I am right. I am giving him credit for that. The government for at best a year or two of power will capitulate to the free trade element of the country, for let it be understood, and it will be understood, that the present proposed reduction in the tariff is only a beginning. The western farmer will experience but slight relief because of this reduction. Our manufacturers are appalled. The Progressive party is not going to stop at this reduction; other manufactured articles, including shoes, clothing and furniture will be next in line.
What person or company will embark in enterprise in this country with the sword of Damocles hanging over their heads. It is impossible to get capital to engage in enterprise unless they have some guarantee that there will not be a continual tinkering with our tariff. A short time ago hon. gentlemen will remember a bond issue of fifty million dollars was subscribed readily in this country
The Budget-Mr. Dickie

out of capital which should under other conditions have been embarked in industrial undertakings or in developing the potentialities of our wonderful country, as has been ably pointed out by the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Ryckman). People are afraid to trust their money in industrial .enterprises and prefer bonds. How can it end? It can only end in disaster for Canada. We must have stability, and if we do not have that stability, I should shudder to think what may become of our country. We have going out yearly to the United States $250,000,000 in excess of what we receive from them. Of that amount $188,000,000 represents our adverse balance of trade with that great country. The balance represents interest on bonds, municipal, provincial and federal, and also interest on American investments in this country. Just think of it, Mr. Speaker, one billion dollars every four years! Is it possible for any nation? Can any nation of nine million people stand an expenditure of one billion dollars going across the line every four years?
That is what is happening to-day, and still in the face of that we are lowering the tariff barriers to that country in order to bring in more importations, and to have a larger amount of our capital go across the line. It is inevitable that we cannot go on indefinitely along these lines. Surely the Progressives have not a monopoly of the economic sanity of the world, the principal nations of which have decided against free trade. I say the principal nations; well nearly all nations have, with the exception of England. And what of poor old England, with a million and a half of unemployed men, her factories idle, her shops filled with cheap articles from continental Europe? Premier Baldwin pointed out the only remedy for a part of England's trouble, but England listened to the voices of the theorists and of demagogues and rejected the advice, and so you have what you see in England to-day.
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) in a recent speech said that the coal mines of Alberta required no artificial stimulation, and that the normal growth would take care of the business for those coal 'mines. I think it would be illuminating to the hon. gentleman if he would only study the history of the iron and steel industry of the United States. That country struggled along for some years. It was impossible for it to compete with England with its great supplies of iron and coal, lying side by side, and with its highly organized industries. Then a heavy duty was imposed on iron and steel coming into the United States. That was found to be inadequate. After a heavier duty was im-

posed, and only when a prohibitive duty was placed on iron and steel was it possible to build up the industry in the United States. Nobody could overrate the importance of that industry, which is recognized as the barometer of trade in the United States to-day. Had the industry not been protected, had the artificial stimulation of which the hon. member for Bow River spoke, not been applied, England would still, or at least until 1914, be sending this iron and steel into the United States.
The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) the other day informed the House that he would like to go over to Wisconsin and buy some heifers. It seems too bad that a man should not be allowed such a small privilege; but if he has heifers or if he has wheat, or cows, or chickens to sell, does he suppose that the people from Wisconsin are coming over to buy from him? They have said plainly and distinctly, through their McCumber tariff that they will not do so. You could not sell one of your cattle over there if you tried. They do not want them there. They say "Keep your tarnation critters off our land. Them is our sentiments, by heck." That is what we hear from his farmer friend across the line.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is the hon. member under
the impression that the member for Lisgar wanted to buy cattle to please the Americans or to please himself?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To please himself. He
wanted to take his money over there, buy cattle, leave his money there and bring the cattle back. I do not think that a man who would deal with a country that absolutely refuses to buy from us displays any great Canadian spirit. A man who, in a Uriah Heep kind of way, goes to the States to buy from them when they will not buy from us is not showing the right spirit. We obviously benefit to a degree from the amount of American capital that is invested in our country. The Americans come in here, and we welcome them They have invested their money and made profits. Those profits go to build up their cities and enhance colossal fortunes across the line. But we do not get as much out of our resources as we should get. On the wild north coast of Scotland there is a humble monument erected over the graves of twenty or more drowned seamen. On the monument is inscribed-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is as old as the hills.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, so are you. On this
monument is inscribed "Erected by Scotchmen to the memory of unknown sailors out

The Budget-Mr. Dickie
of a part of the money found on their bodies." With respect to this money going across the line from the West, I have seen the up-to-date cities of Spokane, Seattle and other cities fostered and become prosperous because of the mineral wealth and money which they have got from our Yukon region and our Kootenay region, money which should have stayed in Canada. Across the line they have an era of prosperity which we do not have in Canada. In days gone by I have seen Los Angeles, when it was smaller, practically thronged with people from the prairie provinces. Those were in the days when they were making money either by speculation or by wheat mining; but many of them were going down there taking with them money which they had accumulated in Canada and making their homes in Los Angeles as they had a perfect right to do. People called them "wheat miners," and the term "wheat miners" is right, because raising wheat year after year means simply mining out of the soil the nitrogenous element which has been years in accumulating. The people in the West must turn to mixed farming. While it would be presumptuous on my part to tell them how to farm or anything relating to agriculture, it is inevitable that they must turn to mixed farming. In San Joaquin and Sacramento valleys in California in the summer you would once see waving fields of wheat, and in the fall, as far as the horizon, you could see blazing stacks of straw. They were taking everything from the land and giving nothing back. The yield fell from 20 to between 5 and 7 bushels an acre, and then the growing of wheat was discontinued. We all remember when the Dakotas were noted for their magnificent wheat, but we hear very little about that now. History will repeat itself in western Canada, and surely the time is at hand when we should conserve our resources. We are raising too much wheat at the present time. Let us take the copper market, in the big mines in the West when the price of copper drops below ten cents a pound, it is impossible to produce copper at a profit. The smelters close down and the mines close down to a certain extent. When consumption overtakes production again and copper goes up to 13 cents a pound, the mines are started again. If the good farmer's of the West could act in a similar way with regard to wheat, they could get $1.50 a bushel for their wheat which is as low as wheat should be sold at. That is the way the thing works out in regard to copper, and I know of no other way in which copper could be worked. Why is that not applicable to the wheat industry? People will say: The
farmers cannot do those things and I believe that may be true. The problem is one that cannot be cured by tariff legislation. In 1921 we imported $24,000,000 worth of agricultural implements into Canada. The duty on those implements does not amount to more than one-third of a cent per bushel on wheat, an absolutely insignificant fraction as regards bringing prosperity to the people of the West. Against that one-third of a cent which they might get, but which I do not consider they would get in the long run, we have the appalling case of manufacturers throughout Canada not knowing which way to turn. These manufacturers are honourable men. We must take their word with respect to the business they engage in. We have their balance sheets which show that they are losing money. Some hon. members feel a little annoyed when the word "manufacturer" is mentioned, and I have even heard the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) emit moans as if in pain when the word "manufacturer" is used. I believe he is an absolutely sincere, lovable gentleman; but it seems to me, living in those great lone prairies with too much time on their hands, these hon. gentlemen to my left have imbibed too many theoretical principles and have not adapted themselves to things that are practical.
As regards free trade, the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) the other day in a few words expressed sentiments regarding free trade that cannot be denied. The hon. member said that were conditions of living equal throughout this world free trade would be	right	and practicable,	but until such
conditions exist, it is not practicable. That is a fact. For	instance, in our
9. p.m. case on the Pacific coast, supposing America were	guaranteed one
hundred years of free trade with the Orient, where do you think your manufactures would go?	Manufacturing establishments would
spring up like mushroons in those countries of the Orient where labour was worth ten or fifteen cents a day. What would happen to our manufacturing centres in this country? The farmers may say: We are farmers; we can live off the land; but we must look at things in a broader light, and I am sure my hon. friends in their quiet moments do so. Up to date, we have used the farmers very decently, I consider, with their agricultural colleges and experimental stations scattered throughout the country and railroad faoilities. Now they want us to build the Hudson Bay railway. Who would build it? Would the cost come out of these gentlemen? It must come out of the industrial parts of Canada, the forests
The Budget-Mr. Dickie

and mines and fisheries of British Columbia, the forests, mines and fisheries of the Maritime provinces, the industries of Quebec and Ontario. How much would the farmers of the three prairie provinces subscribe to the Hudson Bay railway? Nevertheless, they do not seem to have any gratitude in their hearts; they have no consideration for the manufacturer who shows that he has been losing money for years, with his back against the wall, trying to keep his employees together, trying to do something for Canada. Those -.re things that make us at times just a little annoyed with the theories which we hear from hon. members to our left.
Undoubtedly, consideration will be given to them in regard to railway rates. I believe the railway rate from Edmonton to Fort William on wheat is about 24^ cents a bushel. For just one-half the distance over an equally good grade to the city of Vancouver, the rate is 22J cents. Nobody can call that an equitable rate and it must be lowered. The people of the whole of Alberta must have a low wheat rate across the mountains into British Columbia. I do not say that because I am a British Columbian. I am trying to look at all these matters from the standpoint of a Canadian who wants to see our country go ahead, who realises that we are not making the progress that we should make. We are side by side with a magnificent nation to the south of us, a nation that came through the war with half the money in the world and with flying colours. On the other hand, we came through the war, mortgaged up to the hilt, with our young men coming back, battered, and we are fighting up the hill. Let us, like Canadians, turn our backs to the wall to the south and fight in order to make Canada a nation to be proud of.
In order to preserve Canada, let us adopt the only course that is commensurate with dignity and that will make Canada what we wish it to be. That course is to copy other nations, to adopt a protective policy, to nail our colours to the mast. Let the manufacturing interests, let everybody know that these will be our duties twenty years from to-day, and in that way you will see an immediate recovery. Let us make our duties exactly the same against the Americans as those which they have against us. There is not one argument in favour of letting their eggs come into Canada at four cents a dozen while ours go in there at eight cents and our cattle are hardly able to get into the United States at all. They are charging 42 cents a bushel duty on our wheat. I would prohibit every bushel of Canadian wheat from going into the United States. Establish flour fnills in the

West and make the best grade of flour in the world. Advertise that fact. Ship flour, not wheat. Do not allow our No. 1 Northern to go into the United States to raise their grade of wheat in order to make flour that .will compete with ours. Those are bigger things than any tariff tinkerings that have been going on in this House this session. We must stop this exodus of money to the United States. As I have said, we are sending a billion dollars across the line every four years. We cannot stand the strain with a population of 9,000,000. Let us produce and consume our own bacon and coal and let our Progressive friends to our left throw away their can openers and produce more of the commodities that they are buying. It may be presumptuous on my part, and if I am wrong I desire to be corrected; but it struck me in my peregrinations through the prairie provinces that there is a lot of money lost through depreciation in agricultural machinery which is left outdoors exposed to the elements for twelve months of the year. I think that there is lost in this way almost as much as is collected in the way of duty on agricultural implements. I may be wrong in that regard, but I certainly do know that machinery left out in the open in the climate of British Columbia would deteriorate to a very marked degree. Any man who has an elementary' knowledge of oxidation of metals and of the effects of alternate dampness and heat on the wooden parts of machinery will, I think, realize that there is at least some justification for the suggestion I have just made.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that we ought to avoid all racial feeling and creed distinctions, and discard as far as we possibly can any differences of this kind that divide us. What care we what a man is provided he is neither yellow nor red, nor turns his face towards Mecca? If a man is honest and honourable, a white man and a good Canadian citizen, there is no reason whatever why he should not make good in this country. Let us give people credit for sincerity in their beliefs. There is no reason for intolerance in this country, whose people are a splendid race. The people of Quebec, with their charming folk lore and their admirable traditions, and the people of old Ontario, who also have traditions of which they may be proud, are all equally good Canadians, and we do not want any line of demarcation between them. I am sure, too, that the people of the prairie provinces are among our finest citizens. It is therefore humiliating, Mr. Speaker, to hear people raising cries of racial

The Budget-Mr. Lavigueur
and other differences. This to me seems cowardly and I think we ought to put our backs to the wall and endeavour to make Canada a country to be proud of.
If I have said anything in the course of my remarks that might be construed as a criticism of the business methods of our American friends I take this opportunity to disabuse the minds of hon. members of any such impression, for I have every respect for the American people and am heartily in accord with their tariff policy. I believe that policy a wise one which should be followed by the Canadian people. The Americans have prospered under it, and other countries have adopted it; and here we are tinkering with the tariff, reducing the duty a little here and there, in the endeavour to placate an element that could be pleased in a larger way without such concessions, which have the effect of disturbing the whole industrial activity of the country. So far as the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) is concerned, I really do not think that it calls for any discussion.
Mr. HENRI E. LAVIGUEUR (Quebec
County):	It is customary to congratulate
the Minister of Finance who has delivered the budget upon the excellence of his performance, and on the present occasion I take great pleasure in associating myself with my hon. friend (Mr. Dickie) in tendering to the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) my sincere congratulations on the very able manner in which he has discharged the duties of the office this year. In the budget speech there are a few announcements which I think will reassure the people of this country, and the present government Reserve every commendation on the way in which they have adjusted the finances so as to make possible the promise of a surplus in the administration of the affairs of Canada. It is also a great comfort to learn that the burden which has been bearing so heavily upon the shoulders of the taxpayers is diminishing to some extent. One practical instance of this is the reduction which has been made in the sales tax. It has been wiped out in some instance and on 'the whole has been reduced from 6 to 5 per cent. True, it is not a great reduction, but I think it may be regarded as a step in the right direction. The present government assumed a very serious obligation in 1921 and they have succeeded in greatly improving the condition of the country. The policy which has been followed by them is one that appeals to the Canadian people, the policy of retrenchment and economy.
If I say that the budget in some of its aspects is a great satisfaction to the people of Canada, I must confess on the other hand that there is undoubtedly an unsettled feeling in regard to tariff reductions, and the manufacturing element is somewhat alarmed as to what will be the future policy of the government. I understand that the reduction on agricultural implements is well received by the agricultural classes of the country, who are the great mass of our citizens and who are a deserving body. A compensation has been offered the manufacturers of agricultural implements by putting upon the free list the raw material that goes into the making of this machinery; and the sales tax has also been removed from this line of manufactured goods. In Quebec city we have a lot of important shoe factories, and as I have already stated, those interested in them are somewhat alarmed, not so much by what is contained in the budget as by certain remarks made by some influential members of the government. The hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), in the speech he made on the budget, said, as reported on page 1337 of Hansard:
One could not help but be struck this afternoon, in listening to the address of the ex-Finance Minister (Sir Henry Drayton) by the fact that he saw very little wrong with the budget as presented on this occasion, but it was interesting to note the desperate way in which the hon. member declared that it was the death knell of protection. One would have thought that we were listening to a funeral oration this afternoon, and I trust that it will be the death knell of protection. I do not mean to suggest for a single moment that we should vote at this time to abolish the tariff in its entirety, but rather that we should do as we have been doing,-as to w'hich my hon. friend complained so bitterly-continually amend the tariff where it bears too heavily upon the production of the country.
Mr. Speaker, in addition to that declaration of the hon. Minister of the Interior we have the pronouncement of the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) who stated that he would be quite willing to abolish the tariff on boots and shoes. I wish to put myself on record, as a Liberal member supporting the government and a representative of the province of Quebec and the district of Quebec, that we do not share the views of the hon. Minister of the Interior and of the hon. member for Pontiac. We have nothing to complain about in the tariff as it is now, but if I might be permitted to make a suggestion to the government I would ask them to have more protection as regards the British preference in the matter of shoes which are brought in here and which compete with the product of our shoe factories in the province of Quebec. I would suggest also that the sales tax, which has been diminished

The Budget-Mr. Lavigueur
from 6 per cent to 2\ per cent on shoes, should be entirely eliminated from that product and imposed to the extent of 5 per cent on imported shoes, so as to show our industries that we are willing to protect them, and also to do away with the feeling of uncertainty which prevails among those engaged in this class of manufacture. As I said a moment ago, I am not partial in my views; I think it is our duty to protect the agricultural interests and it is our duty also to protect the industries of our country. I think the budget as a whole should be well regarded by the citizens of Canada, because it contains many announcements which should be well received.

I wish to tender my congratulations to the government upon their policy of economy and retrenchment. I am in favour of that policy, but I am in favour of real economy. We in the province of Quebec and especially in the district of Quebec and Quebec city are quite willing to put up with the situation; if there is no money to be spent, no work to be done through tout the country, we are quite willing to make our sacrifice as we have made it for a number of years. But there are very important works that are urgently required and should be proceeded with in my city and in my district. In the constituency which I have the honour to represent in this House we have made, several demands and we hope that they will yet be carefully considered and that justice will be done in respect to them.
I am in favour of economy and retrenchment, and I must confess that I am some-fMr. Lavigueur.]
what astonished at the great amount of money which we are being asked to vote for branch lines. I know that a good many of these new branch lines are probably essential to the good administration of the Canadian National Railways, but we are told that many of them could be delayed for some time without the railways suffering. If we had retrenchment in this matter of branch lines, probably the district and province of Quebec would not have been refused for years its just demands for most essential works. With the money that is being spent on some of these branch lines, which could be delayed for some time without the railways suffering, a good many very necessary works in the district and province of Quebec could be proceeded with. Lately I have been asking the government to repair or rebuild the sustaining wharf f>r St. Gregoire, which was built by the government, at government expense, and has been maintained by the government since 1905, but as yet we have not been able to succeed in getting a grant of money to repair this wharf. At Loretteville, which is a very important centre, we have been asking for the erection of a post office. We have also been asking for the erection of a post office at Beauportville, which is also very necessary, but the answer to our demands has always been that the government has no money. 1 hope that these demands will be seriously considered by the government and that the necessary provision for these works will be made in the supplementary estimates.
Another very essential work is the building of a bridge from the island of Orleans to the north shore, where the people in six very important parishes are without any means of communication whatever. I understand, of course, that the government itself cannot build a bridge, but a subsidy could be granted to help in the building of a bridge at this point, just as was done in the case of the bridge from Isle Perrot to Montreal. All these demands have been pressed upon the government, and a good many other demands by members from that district, but they have not been satisfied yet. We do not wish to blame the government, but I think the time has come when the government should seriously consider these demands and do something for the province of Quebec which has. sent here sixty-five members out of a possible sixty-five. The citizens of the province of Quebec are counting for something upon this government, which we have maintained in power since 1921. I do not want to be too severe on the government and no one will contend that I have been. I am a supporter of the government; I have always been faithful to the government; and

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The budget
speech of this year is of particular interest on account of the reference in the Speech from the Throne to "tariff re-adjustments" and the statement that "reduction of taxation should aim primarily at reducing the cost of the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion."
That statement was construed in the public mind to mean a reduction of some kind in the case of agricultural implements. We are told in press reports that when a deputation from the makers of agricultural implements waited on the Prime Minister protesting any reduction in duties, he told them he could not understand why they should! surmise that a reduction of duty was intended'; as a change in, or abolition of the sales tax would have the effect referred to in the address.
Manufacturers, factory workmen and the inhabitants of the cities generally had the word of the Prime Minister, given during the 1921 election campaign, that despite the tariff platform of 1919, he could give them the assurance that, to use his own words "Our tariff is a tariff for revenue. No legitimate industry in this country, making a legitimate profit, need have any concern one way or the other as to what will happen to its future under Liberal policy in the administration of the tariff." He mnde that statement 94
November 5, 1921, in my city where he spoke in favour of the Liberal candidate who professed adherence to what he called the "Laurier-Fielding tariff." The Prime Minister also made the same statement in the city of Brantford, which is, according to the hon. member for that city, the home of the agricultural implement industry. Other members have referred to that statement being made elsewhere.
Now, for two sessions of this parliament, although many minor changes were made, no changes of a sweeping character took place. It is true that the customs duties on many lines of agricultural implements were reduced 2i per cent in 1922, but those changes were almost completely nullified by the changes made in the sales tax at that time. The sales tax was placed at 41 per cent on Canadian manufactured goods, and 6 per cent on all goods imported, the difference of 11 per cent just about making up the loss of protection by the reduction made in the tariff. That legislation remained in force until January 1st of this year when by the legislation of 1923 the sales tax was made operative at 6 per cent on all sales. So that within a few months the makers of agricultural implements face a varying reduction in customs duties of 21 plus 4 per cent, and in some cases 121 per cent, actually a reduction of from 61 to 121 Per cent.
For the first two sessions there was some uncertainty as to the course the government proposed to follow. Then came the statement made in the budget speech last year by the finance minister guaranteeing, as everyone who heard or read it supposed, reasonable tariff stability. Surely that statement was made in all sincerity, and with the object of promoting confidence in the minds of business men as to the intention of the government? Time works changes, and the "personnel of the famous compass" has undergone some variation. The finance minister who guaranteed tariff stability, and the former Minister of Justice who was never uncertain in his utterances on the tariff question have given place to others. Adverse by-elections have deprived the government of its majority. The Prime Minister has appealed to the Progressive party for support, and one form of the appeal, is shown in the reduction of customs tariff on agricultural implements. How will the Prime Minister explain the utter repudiation of last year's tariff stability announcement by the right hon. gentleman who still retains the title of Minister of Finance? How will he explain the pronouncement of his own in 1921 in relation to legitimate industries making



The Budget-Mr. White
legitimate profits? He will surely not say that the agricultural implement industry, the iron and steel industry, the paint industry, or the boot and shoe industry, are not legitimate forms of activity for Canadian business men. The business men and the workmen of Canada are entitled to an explanation concerning these things. It would appear that the only explanation is that in order to remain in power the Prime Minister has submitted to dictation by the Progressive party, and the Progressive group is now the dominant one in this House. Perhaps the members of the government will tell the House and the country whether or not they have surrendered to the Progressives, or are they starting to give effect to the 1919 declaration of policy. In either case, it seems, the result will be the same. We have the example of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) rising in his place and saving that, he "hoped the present tariff changes will mean the death knell of protection." We had the member for Dufferin (Mr. Wood) congratulating the government on the changes they had made, saying that the ship of state was proceeding in the right direction but they were looking for greater changes in the protective tariff. All the changes are to be downward according to the Whip of the Progressive party and none up. Then we have the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) who gloried in the fact that a real accomplishment had been recorded and that there was now a line of demarcation between the two old parties.
Business in Canada has been halting for some time. Last fall when the Dominion government loan of 8200,000,000 and the Ontario government loan of 840,000,000 were floated, they were both over-subscribed. Newspapers commented on this as an indication that Canada had plenty of money to invest, and that business was sound and industries prosperous. In my judgment, that rush to secure government bonds was proof that business and industry were not in a healthy condition. It was proof that business and industry were not attractive enough to capital to compare with a government offer of a return of about 5i per cent on the investment. Instead of investing our capital in developing our natural resources we are lending to ourselves at the expense of our industrial activities, a practice which, if persisted in and enlarged is not likely to make us more prosperous than taking in each other's washing. Only a short time ago it was announced in the press that the Ontario Minister of Mines will visit England shortly to try to induce investments from that quarter.

Further proof of the decline in business is furnished by a perusal of the revenue resulting from income tax, which, for the eleven months preceding March 1 last, compared with a similar period in 1922, shows a loss of 85,296,000 odd, and business tax compared with the same period shows a loss of 87,438,000 odd, a loss of twelve and three-quarter millions on the two items of direct taxation which must accurately reflect the general condition of business. Of failures in manufacturing in Canada we had in 1920, 255; in 1921, 599; in 1922, 857; and in 1923, 792, I think it was.
In the city of London, which I have the honour to represent, we have many factories. The last government enumeration of Canadian industries credited us with nearly four hundred factories, with over 11,000 people employed therein. Our factories are nearly all working below capacity or on short hours. For example, one factory making farm machinery which a few years ago employed three hundred1 men now has but thirty on its pay roll; another, in the iron and steel industry employing over one thousand, is running short time and not averaging five days per week; another employing 150 men is working four days per week-and so it goes. The matter is considered of so serious a nature that our city council, on the 17th March last, passed a resolution which I should like to have recorded. The resolution is as follows:
Whereas at the present time there are unsettled business and industrial conditions in Canada and an exodus of skilled mechanics and workmen to the United States, which is alarming in proportions;
And whereas the United States has to-day an ultrahigh protective tariff, while Canadian industry has in addition to face competition from countries with depreciated currency and lower standards of living;
Be it resolved that this council regrets the intimation in the Speech from the Throne that the government intends to reduce further the duties on certain manufactured articles, and urges the government rather to take such steps as will protect and stabilize the industries of the Dominion so as to give permanent and assured employment to Canadians in Canada; and that the City Clerk be instructed to write to the Right Honourable Mackenzie King, Premier, to the Hon. Jas. A. Robb, Acting Minister of Finance, and the member for London, calling their attention to this resolution.
S. Baker,
City Clerk.
I think there are many indications that capital has been timorous, afraid to venture, fearful of the risks incident to investment in industry, and that fear is accentuated to-day by the abandonment of the principle of tariff stability and the substitution of a policy of attrition, which the government is asking the House to sanction. While the provisions of the budget create a serious situation for many

The Budget-Mr. White
workmen and many manufacturing companies, the most serious effect of these tariff changes will be, in my opinion, the effect on business generally.
Canadian people will remember that the Liberal platform, which is almost identical with that of the Progressive group, contains many provisions regarding the reduction of duties, the increase in British preference and a long list of articles to be placed on the free list. What incentive is there for new capital to go into business, or what incentive is there for a manufacturing concern already established to plan for an enlargement of buildings or plant or to make efforts to employ additional workmen when the prospect is that the axe will fall again next year, when the budget is delivered, in all probability with greater severity? The country knows that the Progressive group, encouraged by the comparatively small success of this year will likely be more insistent next year and demand a much larger and more comprehensive reduction of protective duties, and the country also knows that the government which gave way this year will likely acquiesce next year.
On Tuesday, April 14, the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) made the statement that he hoped the tariff on boots and ehoes would be lowered, and in twelve hours a deputation of sixty or seventy men from his own province and Ontario representing the boot and shoe manufacturers and the workmen in that industry, appeared, asking for protection from the competition of English and German goods particularly. They asserted that Canada has factory capacity for 25,000,000 pairs of shoes per annum, while the Canadian market consumes about 15,000,000 pairs; also that English firms on account of lower wage costs and the depreciation of currency, more favourable freight rates and the increase in the British preference last year, had secured a large portion of Canadian business. Will the Prime Minister say that the boot and shoe industry is not a legitimate industry as far as Canada is concerned?
When that deputation presented its case it also called on two of its members who represented labour, to state the case for labour. These men represented both the Catholic Workers Union, and the International Shoe Workers Union. They appealed Jto the government for protection from foreign competition, so that the factories in which they are employed would be able to work at greater capacity and at full time. They had been assured by the minister from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Sinclair) in his 94i
speech in the House a day or two before that this is a wonderfully successful government. They had been assured that a great accomplishment had been recorded in the direction of economy. The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) undertook to convince this deputation, which if they know anything at least know their own business, that the Canadian workers were not suffering more than ordinarily, and if I can judge by the expression on the faces of these men they were comparing the short time of the shoe factories with the statement of the minister without portfolio, who asserted that their taxes were to be reduced this year by the sum of $2.70 per man. Perhaps they were wondering what they would do with this $2.70, whether they would spend it all at once, or extend it over several celebrations during the year.
The Liberal party in the 1921 campaign expressed great concern for the welfare of the labouring man. They were quite in sympathy with the conventions of the League of Nations including the shorter working day; they were going to grant all these concessions to the working man, and they have been giving to them the shorter week with a vengeance!
The government is making no effort to check the exodus of Canadian workmen to the United States. We are told that 181,000 of these workmen left Canada last year. The Prime Minister made the assertion that he believed sixty per cent of these had returned. I have had a great deal to do with workmen, I know something of them in my own city, and if six per cent of them returned I think that would be about the extent of it. In fact I am very dubious about the six per cent. I have encountered very few men who have gone over to the States within the last, two years and have returned. Those men are^ leaving the country because the work is-being done in the United States and the manufactured goods are being imported into ada. They left Canada because Canada did not provide them with the living they thought they were entitled to. They believed they could provide themselves with a better living by going to the United States. Some day they may come back when the conditions of industry are improved by wise legislation, but in the meantime our loss is the gain of the United States.
As to the effect of the changes in the customs duties on the manufacture of agricultural implements in Canada, I believe that only the manufacturers of implements can make a forecast. Taking into consideration the change in the sales tax which I referred

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Gentlemen, the session which opened on the 12th January 1916, will ever be a memorable one for the parliamentarians of that year. The great world war was raging. The hopes entertained after the battle *of the Marne for an early collapse of the enemy forces had been shattered. Though the Allies had won notable victories-in which the sons of Canada had by sacrifice of blood and of life performed deeds of which the glory shall never fade away-yet the march towards the Rhine was checked in that they had failed to pierce the German lines. On the eastern front, our disappointments had been still greater. The only bright spot at the horizon was the effective watch and patrol of the British Navy which left the German fleet impotent and imprisoned in its own waters. Sad as the immediate prospects were, the spirit of the Canadian people remained undaunted. And their representatives in parliament, undismayed by the ghastly welter of blood and fire, resolved to stand by the gallant soldiers who at Ypres, Festubert and 'Givenchy, had fought and died for a noble cause and to carry on until final victory.
Whilst under the shadow of those stirring events, when the House of Commons was engaged in the all absorbing task of securing more men and assessing more resources to prosecute the war, a sudden and appalling disaster happened here on the hill. On the 3rd of February at nine o'clock in the evening, during the course of one of those week end debates with which we are so familiar, the parliament buildings were destroyed by fire.

It was a noble edifice; indeed, it was a landmark. There, half a century before, as a result of the Quebec Conference had gathered the leaders who after merging their interests in common had launched the newly bom union. There, had been sealed the pact of confederation. As we gazed at the next sunrise at the mass of black ruins, projecting its distress upon the wide fields of snow, as we looked in vain for the stately tower which crowned the beautiful structure, the quaint gables, the gothic arches and the stained glass windows around which clung so many memories, there was a deep feeling of sorrow. But these, after all, were only material things.
Far more deplorable was the loss of life- and we are assembled here to-day, eight years after that calamitous event, at the gates of a new parliament to officially record the profound affection in which one of the victims, Bowman Brown Law, member for the constituency of Yarmouth, was held by us all, his fellow members.
For many years, it was my privilege to sit in the House of Commons with him. Quiet and unassuming	in his	bearing,	gentle	inhis manners, he was none the less a very industrious member, attentive to his duties and well informed. Scarcely an hour had elasped on that	fateful	evening,	when	hisvoice had been	raised	on behalf of	hiselectors. As usual, he had spoken in all earnestness, on	a question of primary
importance to Nova Scotia, a province renowned for the inborn ability and common sense of its people.
A God-fearing gentleman, a true Canadian, a devoted and loving husband and father, a faithful and trusted servant of the people, such was Bowman Brown Law.-
This tablet will recall to his family and his constituency that, at this very spot, where he so tragically entered in the valley of the shadow, his memory survives;-the sweet memory of one whom we know through his life training, faced bravely the awful ordeal, which he accepted in a Christian spirit, as only a preface to that reward in the realm beyond, where the soul is greeted by a merciful Maker in the white radiance of eternity.
I will now ask the right hon. Prime Minister to say a few words and proceed to the unveiling of the memorial tablet.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Upon the re-assembling of parliament, at the commencement of the present session, there was unveiled the first, monument to be placed in our reconstructed buildings. It was appropriate that it should

The Law Memorial
be to the memory of an honourable member of the House of Commons who lost his life on the field of battle in the service of his king and country overseas. To-day as we re-assemble, after a brief Easter vacation, we are about to unveil a memorial tablet to the memory of another honourable member of the Commons who lost his life under circumstances which also were alike tragic and historic.
The late Bowman Brown Law was first returned to the House of Commons as the member for Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, at a by-election in December 1902, which byelection was occasioned by a vacancy caused by the appointment of the late Mr. T. B. Flint as Clerk of the House. Mr. Law was re-elected at the General Elections of 1904, 1908 and 1911. In the great fire which on February 3, 1916, destroyed the old parliament buildings, he was burned to death. Seven lives in all were lost in that fire, and it is something of a sad coincidence that among the number should have been that of the Clerk Assistant of the House, the late Mr. J. K. Laplante.
Members who enjoyed the privilege of serving in parliament during the years I have mentioned, will recall Mr. Law as a man possessed of singularly fine qualities, alike o heart and mind. He was of a quiet and retiring disposition, affable and companionable. and most punctilious and conscientious in the discharge of his public duties. He was in his seat in the Commons chamber when the alarm of the fire was given, and it is believed that it was in the effort to save from destruction papers in his possession that he took a risk which proved to be fatal.
The memorial tablet which I have now the honour to unveil records the essential facts in the fewest possible words:

maintopic: ERECTED TO THE MEMORY OF BOWMAN BROWN LAW, M.P.   REPRESENTATIVE OF THE COUNTY OF YARMOUTH, N.S. WHO MET HIS DEATH IN THE GREAT FIRE WHICH DESTROYED THE PARLIAMENT BUILDINGS,

speechtext: 3rd FEBRUARY, 1916.

The sculptor has succeeded in executing in bronze relief a remarkably good likeness of the late Mr. Law. To the left, near the top, he has reproduced the coat of arms of the United States, commemorative of the circumstance that Mr. Law was born in the state of Massachusetts; to the right the 
coat of arms of the province of Nova Scotia, the province with which his public career was so closely identified; and over all, the arms of Canada, the country he served so
well-	, .
It is fitting that we should thus preserve and seek to honour the memory of one of our number whose life and whose death were so closely identified with our parliament. The circumstances of Mr. Law's death permitted no place of burial to his mortal remains. They knew no sepulchre save the ruins of the demolished walls within which he met his fate. His ashes mingle with the ashes of the edifice in which for over thirteen years he represented faithfully and well the interests of his constituency and the people of this land. Of him, too, it may truly be said that he died in the service of king and country- In association with his name and memory this, our Westminster, will be not less the Abbey, than the Houses of Parliament.
By fire and the sword, such was the manner of death of those of our number whose memories we have sought to preserve. These mute memorials are imperfect symbols at best. Surrounded as we are by the material evidences of the spirit of resurrection which these reconstructed buildings afford, it may be not without consolation to those who have been bereaved to recall the association which this tablet, placed as it is, will ever bear to the Easter season. To them and to us let it speak of the unfinished tasks of those who are gone, not as of a work that is ended, but as of a greater work begun.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Mr. Prime Minister, ladies and gentlemen: The inclusion of my name in the ceremony of this afternoon testifies chiefly to the fact that this event has no significance narrower than the whole bounds of parliament and of Canada. No words of mine could possibly add to the expressions of profound regard which fell in such beautiful diction from the lips of Mr. Speaker this afternoon, nor to the fine eulogy uttered by the Prime Minister.
My personal association with Mr. Law was of limited kind. He had entered parliament many years before myself, and had not come in that close contact with me which I would have desired. But looking back to the sad hour that we commemorate now I well recall the tragic night-how, after only one hour of deliberation in the evening, the flames were discovered spreading with almost uncanny rapidity, how the mellow hue of the sky was reddened to angry flame, and this splendid edifice destroyed.
The Law Memorial

You spoke, Mr. Speaker, of the times, heavy and poignant, through which we were passing then. These need' sometimes to be recalled. Nevertheless there was something of a lull at the front, at the very time of this fire. During the winter months, a silencing in some degree of the uproar of conflict had fallen, only, of course, to be resumed in all its horror and slaughter when summer weather came. Likewise on the 3rd February, 1916 a peaceful frosty nightfall, as tranquil an evening as we had ever known, was converted into a night of disaster and death.
We had hoped that the former magnificent parliament buildings, would have remained with us as a tribute to the courage and the vision of our forefathers, a courage and a vision greater than we can very well now encompass. The Canada of that day was weak and scattered compared with the nation as we know it now. We had all hoped that those wonderful buildings would have remained as a legacy to our children, an historic legacy joining the old colonial days with the later days which have witnessed the fruition of this Dominion. This we were denied. The awful disaster of February 3rd lost to us the greatest single material possession of which Canada could boast. But appalling as our loss of that nature was, we lament infinitely more bitterly and lastingly the loss of life. Seven persons, as the Prime Minister has said, were imprisoned in the burning building and died. Three of them were servants of the House. Two were lady visitors of the then Speaker. Another victim was one of our most trusted, one of our most competent officers, Mr. Laplante, the then Clerk Assistant. It is in honour of the seventh that we unveil this tablet to-day and in my judgment properly so. Mr. Law was one of our number and naturally, we feel toward his memory an affection nearer and deeper than that which attaches to others. Fitting it is that with respect to him, as to any hon. member who may die in similar tragic manner in the service of his country, the present noble building should contain a memorial-a memorial that will carry down his memory to the latest generations. He and those others have taken their places in the Golden Chamber but they have left to us the memory of creditable lives, the inspiration of splendid examples. Nothing better can be said of Mr. Law, or indeed of any man than that he died as he had lived, a British gentleman at his post of duty.

Mr. Chairman. In common with those who are associated with me on this platform, I am not in a position to say anything that would adequately portray the feelings of those whom 
I represent in reference to the purpose for which we have met here this afternoon.
However, as has been pointed out, in 1916 an incident occurred which might be described as a national calamity, the destruction of the parliament buildings. I can very well remember the occasion when, a few years previous to that time, I had the privilege of visiting the chamber and looking over the seats of the various members of the House, ihe parliament buildings seemed to me then to symbolize the spirit of nationhood, and the burning of that great structure could only be termed a national calamity. But we had an opportunity to repair our loss; the material loss could be overcome, and now a new building has been erected, which is magnificent in every aspect. While we regret the fact that the buildings were destroyed we can now look ack to the event with equanimity, as the building could be replaced and its destruction perhaps in time almost forgotten. But the loss of life is an entirely different matter. V\ e have lost something that can never be restored to us, and we are met this afternoon to unveil a tablet to the memory of one of the members of the House of Commons, who lost his life in that tragic disaster.
I had not the privilege of being acquainted with Mr. Law but we know he was a man in the full vigour of manhood, who could have looked forward to many years of usefulness and service to his country had it not been that m one tragic moment his life was cut short and he was taken away to be amongst us no more.
We look upon death perhaps as one of the greatest calamities that can come to human beings; but there are some things which are sadder than death. When we lose one whom we can respect and admire, whom we can truly love, we have something left, a memory that we can cherish, which may become one of the most sacred things in our lives. This gentleman was lost to the country and to this House, but through all time we can cherish the memory of one who served his country well, who lived a noble life, and who was in every respect a gentleman whom we could respect and admire.
I am very happy to have the privilege of taking part in this ceremony and paying my respects to the memory of one who died in the service of his country.
Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Pictou) (Minister of National) Defence):	Mr. Chairman,
I had the great pleasure and distinction of having served in this House of Commons for a period of eleven years in conjunction with our friend, Mr. Law, whose memory we are

The Law Memorial
commemorating to-day, and of having served for a period of seven years with his father who represented the same constituency in the provincial legislature of Nova Scotia. Mr. Law was my personal friend, and we were associated very closely, coming to this House almost at the same period. Those of us who come from our province, who had the opportunity of knowing Mr. Bowman Law perhaps in a closer way than our confreres from other parts of Canada, know what a typical Nova Scotian he was in many ways. He was a most successful business man, and having inherited from his father a prosperous business organization, he dealt with that in a way which indicated his great ability along those lines. He received the confidence of the people amongst whom he lived as a young man, and in every election when he came to them and asked for a renewal of their confidence, he received it in a greater degree than previously.
I always recall, with horror, the events of that night, February 3. I happened to be in the House at the time, and I well remember the circumstances. Almost in the twinkling of an eye the chamber was surrounded by flames. I personally succeeded in getting to my room and securing some papers, and as I was going to my room, I met Bowman Law coming from his. He apparently had endeavoured, when he reached the ground floor, to go to his locker where his coat, hat and other things were, and nobody ever saw him again. We did not know even that he was dead for two days. It was not until Saturday afternoon that somebody began to inquire where Mr. Law was, and then we realized that this quiet gentleman, who went about his affairs so unostentatiously, was a victim of the fire.
I had an opportunity in conjunction with my colleagues from the province of Nova Scotia of saying a few words about him at a meeting of the House of Commons which took place in the Victoria Museum on the following Monday. A singular circumstance which I recall in Connection with that fact was that on that day the then Prime Minister, Sir Robert Borden, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier both in most eloquent speeches spoke to a resolution of appreciation of the services of Sir Charles Tupper who was a typical Nova Scotian and one of the great men of the Dominion of Canada. Bowman Law's name was referred to by his colleagues at that time.
Those of us who knew him have wonderful memories of him. He was a sincere and straightforward advocate of the rights of his province and of the Dominion. He was a
devoted party man; he was sincerely devoted to the party with which he had so long been associated. He was successful in business to a degree greater than is the lot of most men. During his parliamentary career he gave of his best on behalf of his constituents and province. He was a man of charming disposition, a splendid friend, and those of us who were associated with him will ever have kindly memories of him.
I am sure this tablet which the Prime Minister has to-day unveiled will be a mark for all time to come of him who passed away in that holocaust of February 3, a man who did his duty to his country, who was loyal to his friends, who was a devoted parent and whose memory will ever be cherished, not only by those of us who come from the same province, but those who come from other parts of Canada as well.

speakeroldname: Mr. P. L. HATFIELD (Yarmouth and Clare):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ladies and gentlemen,
having the honour to represent in the House of Commons the constituency which the late Mr. Bowman B. Law represented at the time of his death, I think perhaps it is fitting that I should offer a few remarks at this ceremony. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for having afforded me the opportunity of doing so. I am sure the occasion which brings us together this afternoon must be one unique in the memory of the oldest parliamentarian here. I believe the records of the Canadian parliament will reveal no other instance in which a member of the House of Commons met death under circumstances so tragic and sad as those that surrounded the death of the late Mr. Law. As has been so well explained by you, Mr. Speaker, the late Mr. Law represented in the House of Commons the constituency which at the time of his death was known as Yarmouth; and I am sure that no member of parliament ever enjoyed the confidence and respect and-may I not add-the affection of the electorate throughout the entire length and breadth of his constituency, to a greater degree than did Mr. Law. Judging from the many eulogies I have heard of him since coming here, from his old colleagues and those who were attached to the government service, who knew him, I am sure that the same happy, genial, unselfish disposition which characterised his private life among his constituents must also have been characteristic of his official life here in Ottawa.
As I turn now more directly to the ceremony which is being conducted this afternoon, I must confess that I find it diffi-
The Law Memorial

cult to command language adequately and properly to express my feelings. Assembled as we are on the very spot where that terrible tragedy was enacted, and under the influence of the solemn act of unveiling this memorial tablet which has been erected to Mr. Law's memory, what has been said, and the manner of the saying of it, make it difficult indeed for one to control one's emotions. Mr. Law and I were very close personal friends; and what I have witnessed here and heard this afternoon makes me feel, at least in a large measure, the same sense of loss and shock which we all experienced when we first heard the news of the terrible accident that caused the loss of our friend. My thought turns to the late widow of Mr. Law, who survived her husband for so comparatively short a time. She mourned her loss intensely, and without doubt it was the primary cause of her decease so soon after that of him whom she loved so dearly. She bore her trouble with great patience and fortitude; but to those who were nearest her it soon became evident that the blow had proven too heavy and that she would soon be released from her sufferings here to join him who for so long had been her partner and companion in life. I also think of the daughter who is unavoidably deprived of the opportunity of being present, and for whom I am commissioned to speak. It shall be my duty to portray to her, as faithfully as I can, the esteem and affection in which her departed father was held here by all who knew him; and how his memory is honoured. I am sure that the kindly, gracious words which have been spoken to-day, so tenderly and sincerely, by you, Mr. Speaker, and by the other gentlemen who have followed you, will prove a comfort indeed to her, and if possible will render the memory of him whom she loved so dearly even more sacred and sweet than the memory she has cherished of him in the past. On her behalf I desire to thank you, Sir, and through you the senators and the members of the House of Commons, for this very worthy act which marks so well the passing of one who was loved by all, who represented so faithfully the constituency of Yarmouth and who endeared himself so peculiarly to all who knew him. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will read one or two telegrams which I have received on the subject of this afternoon's ceremony, and which it seems appropriate I should read:

Yarmouth, N.S.

House of Commons,
Ottawa.
The members of the Liberal Association of the constituency of Yarmouth and Clare desire to express to the senators and members of the House of Commons their grateful appreciation for the splendid tribute to their late representative, Bowman Brown Law, in erecting a tablet to his memory in the lobby of the House of Commons. Mr. Law at the time he met his death in the great fire which destroyed the parliament building had long represented our constituency in the House of Commons and was our trusted friend and colleague. Meeting his death while in the performance of his public duties with many years of service ahead of him the memorial service which you are holding to-day strikes a very responsive chord in all our hearts and we look upon it as a splendid tribute to his family as well as to the memory of a true man and faithful public servant.
